subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACTION AGAINST PARTICIPANTS IN OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this day of protest by the Canadian Labour Congress is in fact deemed to be a general strike by a minority, illegal in many parts of the nation, and damaging not only to our economy but to the very essence of our democratic way of life, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That the government take all necessary and appropriate disciplinary action against the instigators of this general strike, in particular Joe Morris, president of the CLC, and other top union officials.

subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence today of the Minister of Labour I wonder if I could direct my question to the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that yesterday the Minister of Labour refused to say whether the government views the national strike as legal but went on to say by implication that it would be illegal unless the protest took place at lunch hour or off-working hours, and in view of conflicting decisions yesterday in different provinces which resulted in the strike being legal in British Columbia and not in Ontario, and given the well publicized fact that working people and others have been concerned about whether illegal action was appropriate in our democratic system, can the Prime Minister now advise whether he or his ministers or any of them ever asked for and obtained legal advice indicating that this strike would be legal in some provinces and not legal in others.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not for the Government of Canada to decide what is legal or not in particular provinces from the point of view of provincial law and collective agreements under provincial labour legislation. The federal position as stated by the minister, which is quite clear, is that if the protest does not involve illegal actions then the Minister of Labour said he could understand the right of individuals or associations to protest policies that they disagreed with by protesting in a legal way; in other words, if they protest by demonstrating during their lunch hour or after their hours of work. If on the contrary they are breaking a contract, then of course it becomes illegal and the Government of Canada cannot condone it; on the contrary we condemn it.

subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: It is all very well for government members to applaud, Mr. Speaker, but the question is one which all the public is asking. It seems very strange-

subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister then tell this House, in view of the fact that for many months the government has known that the CLC was armed with the authority given it at the May convention to call for a national strike, despite the fact that members of the government did not feel it would take place, why there has been no direction from his Minister of Labour or from the government in general as to what the parameters of this particular form of protest ought to be in order to keep it legal, keeping in mind as the government well knows that this strike would be breaking a great many contracts which were not within federal jurisdiction, and especially in view of the fact that the Minister of Labour has confused the public even more by hoping that the strike would be a success.

subsubtopic: LEGALITY OF OCTOBER 14TH DAY OF PROTEST-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMING TO A DECISION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member must have missed what the Minister of Labour said yesterday. He said quite clearly, as I understood him-and he said this outside the House also-that he could not condone illegal action but there was a way of protesting which was perfectly legal. The hon. member knows this. That is the position of the government. If under federal labour legislation there are any illegal acts we will condemn them, and we reserve the right to act in whatever way is appropriate to correct that situation. That is the federal responsibility and a responsibility which we hope the House supports. But we cannot say what position the provinces will take within areas in their own jurisdiction under laws they have passed. I could give the hon. member an opinion. I suppose it would be much the same as that of the federal government. If provincial labour laws are broken and something illegal is done, then I hope those concerned will be condemned in those particular provinces.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BACKGROUND PAPERS ON WHICFI DECISION TO CONTINUE PROGRAM MAY BE BASED
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BACKGROUND PAPERS ON WHICFI DECISION TO CONTINUE PROGRAM MAY BE BASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. As the protest day is obviously designed in the hope that the government will terminate the wage and price control program at the earliest opportunity, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, further to my question yesterday, whether he would lay before the House his analysis or other documentation which he plans to put to the provinces when he requests an extension of the present agreements with those provinces with respect to the wage and price control program. Will he lay that before the House immediately so that the provinces and ourselves can have a fair chance to review this documentation. Second, do we take from his answer yesterday that he is going to request a two year extension from the provinces?

October 14, 1976
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BACKGROUND PAPERS ON WHICFI DECISION TO CONTINUE PROGRAM MAY BE BASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I pointed out to the hon. gentleman yesterday that the present agreements with the provinces run until April of 1977, which is nearly six months away, and that at the beginning of 1977, in the first months of that year, it obviously will be important, both for the purpose of debate in this House and for the purpose of discussions with the provinces, to talk about the progress of the anti-inflation program at that point and the considerations we would have in mind with respect to extension of those particular agreements. It seems to me to be a lot more sensible to talk to them about the impact of the program as it will have been experienced up to early 1977 on the then current facts rather than setting out the analysis now and talking about that in six months time.
So it is for that reason I pointed out to the hon. gentleman that the discussions will commence early next year. They should be carried on on the basis of the experience up until that time. Of course, the period of extension would be confined by the period of time which has been authorized by this parliament, which at the present date is for another two years.

subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH GOVERNMENT JUSTIFIES PROGRAM
BASIS ON WHICH GOVERNMENT JUSTIFIES PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to put my final supplementary to the Prime Minister. In his random remarks yesterday and in his rationalization of the anti-inflation program he spent some time trying to justify the program on the basis that in his view the CPI had gone down, and that it was not only because of the farm gate prices having declined substantially. Is the Prime Minister aware that the chief factor causing food prices in this country to go down is that the beef farmers have literally been murdered by the price of their product going down 20 per cent in the past year, and is this the only way the government feels it can justify its anti-inflation program?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH GOVERNMENT JUSTIFIES PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the hon. member is making a representation, not asking a question.

subsubtopic: AMOUNT OF WAGE INCREASE FOR UNORGANIZED WORKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance arising out of some of the statements made by the Prime Minister yesterday. I should like to ask the minister whether studies have been made by his department or any other government department or agency to ascertain whether the more than 60 per cent of the labour force which is still unorganized in this country has received wage or salary increases in the past year, and if such studies have been made, can he indicate whether the information shows the size of these increases and whether they were above or below the increase in the cost of living in the past year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: AMOUNT OF WAGE INCREASE FOR UNORGANIZED WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to those under the anti-inflation program the Anti-Inflation Board has been analyzing the rate of increases, and indeed, in its report, which will be made available to the House within a matter of weeks, I expect that the board will probably have something to say about that.
With respect to a more extensive analysis of labour groups which are not covered by the mandatory controls, I would have to say that the board obviously has not. 1 do not know whether my colleague the Minister of Labour could advise in this regard as to whether his department, in its general survey of labour income, could respond to the question put by the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: POSSIBILITY PERMISSIBLE MINIMUM WAGE INCREASE MADE MANDATORY
POSSIBILITY PERMISSIBLE MINIMUM WAGE INCREASE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext: Many of the people who are not organized work for small employers who are not covered by the regulations of the Anti-Inflation Board. In view of the feelings of many people that the anti-inflation program is not being applied fairly, is the government giving consideration to making the minimum increase of $600 a year, which is permitted under the anti-inflation legislation, mandatory in order that employees in the lowest income levels, most of whom do not belong to unions and have no bargaining power, can be helped to cope with the increased cost of living this past year?

subtopic: POSSIBILITY PERMISSIBLE MINIMUM WAGE INCREASE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a very substantial sense a great deal of the work force the hon. gentleman referred to is not under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. With regard to the parliament of Canada, he is asking if it is our intention to increase the minimum wage to $3.50 an hour. I can say that is not the intention at this time.
October 14, 1976

subtopic: POSSIBILITY PERMISSIBLE MINIMUM WAGE INCREASE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext: A final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I had no intention of asking the minister if the government was giving consideration to increasing the minimum wage to $3.50 an hour. 1 want to ask the minister whether the government is giving consideration to, and consulting with the provinces in respect of, jointly raising the minimum wage of employees under their jurisdiction so that the large number of people who are working, many of whom are included in the large number who are still classified as living in poverty by such organizations as the Economic Council of Canada, can be taken out of that poverty group and given a wage on which they can live fairly decently?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can say to the hon. gentleman that both the Minister of Labour and I have continually had discussions with the provincial governments with respect to the level of the minimum wage and there is, of course, quite a spectrum of opinion in Canada as to what the appropriate level should be. As I said, I cannot give any assurance that the minimum wage generally in Canada will be raised either by the federal government or by the ten provincial governments to the level of $3.50 an hour.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS FOR VALDES FAMILY

Mr. Speaker, the situation the hon. member describes he declares to be humanitarian. There are many humanitarian situations outside the country. People endeavouring to enter this country face situations every bit as difficult as those facing the lady and family to which the hon. member refers; but they see fit to obey our laws and make application in the appropriate way instead of attempting to enter the country illegally and then go through a whole series of procedures. The family referred to has been given the benefit of the most generous appeal procedures in the world; it has been looked at carefully. At present there is an application before the court

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGES IN TRIAL PROCEDURES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Justice about a leak, deliberate or otherwise, with respect to recommendations for introducing a bill to abolish preliminary hearings and jury trials, something which goes to the root of the liberty of the subject. I ask the Minister of Justice, who has been quiet about that leak, if he intends during the present session, or in any session, to bring forward a bill in accordance with those recommendations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGES IN TRIAL PROCEDURES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have hardly been quiet. I held a press conference and made public the report to which the hon. member is referring. I made a speech in Vancouver in which I said that we do not intend to interfere with the jury system, the right of the accused to remain silent, and the protection against selfincrimination. The hon. member really was referring to two reports, one being on work done by the Law Reform Commission on pre-trial proceedings, the other being a memorandum for discussion with deputy attorneys general prepared by an official of mine. It related to other matters, namely, how to decrease backlogs in the courts.
Obviously, the suggestions coming from the Law Reform Commission bear the closest examination and scrutiny by all people of this country, including I hope the hon. member, who share my concern that we should, where possible, eliminate delays in the trial process without at the same time interfering with the fundamental rights of the accused. That work is going on, but 1 am not in a position to say at this time whether any bill will be introduced relating to that matter. I have formed no recommendations; I have not made any.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGES IN TRIAL PROCEDURES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question? Since the answer of the Minister of Justice was full of ambiguities, I ask, is he going to introduce a bill? If so, will he refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs? It is a most serious matter, going to the root of the very freedom and liberty of the subject. The right to trial by jury for indictable offences is as old as Magna Carta. Will the minister do as I suggest before the sort of confusion is created that we saw with respect to Bill C-83?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGES IN TRIAL PROCEDURES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to say whether or not a bill will be introduced as not even my own department is yet in a position to make recommendations or suggestions to me. Therefore, I am not in a position to say
October 14, 1976

whether or not a bill will be introduced. If one were to be, obviously, it would be referred to the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. In view of the strong objections voiced by the Montreal business community about the proposal to transfer domestic flights from Dorval to Mirabel airport, does the government intend to put off the planned transfer of those flights until a satisfactory rapid transit system can be built to reduce greatly the time of transit and cost of travel between Mirabel and Montreal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is inaccurate to refer to the situation in relation to traffic going to Mirabel as a planned transfer. We have been investigating the type of traffic moving through Montreal and the two airports, in an attempt to arrange that traffic in due course in a way to suit the convenience of the region and the people in the area served by the airports. The investigation also deals with the desire to make Montreal a very useful interconnection point for passengers from other parts of the country. We are therefore investigating this matter. It is now clear that we will not make any major change for some months; I would say spring is the next possibility. Our real purpose is to meet the convenience of passengers in every way, and we will try to take all factors into account, including surface transport. But that is only one factor which has to be taken into account.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of information coming out of Mirabel today showing that the new airport was not needed in the first place, is it not now evident that this white elephant the government built was both a stupid and costly mistake?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. The increased traffic using Dorval would have created great problems at that airport and for the people of the area.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: All you had to do was extend the terminal facilities.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO TRANSFER FLIGHTS FROM DORVAL TO MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION

I suppose the hon. member is familiar with the kinds of problems which would be created in Toronto for people living near the airport by the expansion of the existing airport. I suppose the hon. member may be familiar with the kinds of problems that would be created for the people living nearby by the expansion of the Toronto airport. The same kind of situation has existed in the case of Dorval.
In addition, the additional land that would have been required would have been extremely costly to expropriate. What we did instead was develop a new airport, which will prove to be an extremely fine example of air service facilities
Oral Questions
in Canada, in an area where we obtained control over an adequate parcel of land to ensure that the kind of problems that developed in other locations will not occur again. Mr. Speaker, before commencing my remarks I want, through you, to congratulate the various hon. members on the government side on the recent positions to which they have been appointed, and wish them well in their endeavours.
I think I might also say they will be watched very closely because it is quite apparent to the Canadian public, and I think certainly to all hon. members who listened to what their constituents had to say during the summer, that there is much uneasiness with the present government and the present approach the government is taking. That uneasiness in my opinion is not just a passing phase but is deeply rooted and stems from a good number of years of not just mismanagement
(Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).]
but no management at all. That lack of management and leadership is the underlying problem the country faces. I say with as much kindness as I can to the new ministers that this is the fundamental task to which they will have to address themselves and that unless they do so the country will not withstand another two years of what we have been through.
I must say I regret that the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) is not here because a personal matter has required that he leave the House. However, I think it would be improper to rise in this debate without stating something bluntly to my friends and colleagues in the New Democratic Party. It is all very well for them to try to take the position on television or in other places that the Conservative Party has no policies or positions. The fact of the matter is that consistently in this House over a good number of years we have said that the country's recovery will depend on productivity, on a competitive market system and a high degree of management-labour accord as well as a close rapport and relationship between government, management and labour. We have said this repeatedly and we have said it in a responsible way. We have said it because it needed to be said since it was not being said by the members of the government or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and certainly was not being said by some of my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party.
It is time that the New Democratic Party and the government began to realize that the public is not impressed with an economy that is stagnant as the result of the mismanagement by the government of the day and partly because of the philosophy and at times utter nonsense uttered by the other opposition party, the New Democratic Party. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party at times, even when it is headed-I was going to use the expression "in the right direction" but they would not like that-in the appropriate direction, handles itself with such complete irresponsibility that it cannot be taken seriously. I am sorry to have to say this as bluntly as I do, but it is true. It was exhibited in the amendment moved yesterday by the New Democratic Party. I wish to read that amendment:
We also affirm that the failure of the government to end the wage and price control program immediately, in light of...
Then, it continues. There is no question but that there are aspects of this wage and price control program with which not only do we, along with our friends from the New Democratic Party, quarrel but which we pointed out would cause trouble at the time the legislation was debated. But it would be completely irresponsible to end the program immediately; that cannot be done and the New Democratic Party ought to know that. So, we have to say we agree with the New Democratic Party that there are inequities in the control program and that it could be and should be improved.
We might take as an example the situation we have in the Yukon Territory at the moment where the Cyprus-Anvil Mining Company achieved an agreement many months ago. The Anti-Inflation Board rolled back the agreed wage scale once, and then changed it. Then, the administrator came in and rolled it back a third time to a lower figure. One result of

all that is that we are very cognizant of the faults in the system. The second result is that there are 400 people who have been and are on strike. The mine is not operating. The business community in Faro is suffering as is the community of Whitehorse. The White Pass and Yukon Railway has cut its operation in half and has laid off 170 drivers. In addition, the government-owned and operated power commission has increased its power rates. Just to make the matter more incredible, the Canadian Labour Relations Board says the strike is legal.
I agree with the New Democratic Party when members of that party point to this sort of thing and say it is not logical. We, of course, have said over and over again that it is not logical. Members of this party were in the forefront in respect of the situation in Thompson, Manitoba and every member of the New Democratic Party knows this. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no doubt that, so far as all members of the House are concerned, there is a very serious situation in the country in the relationship or lack of relationship between employers and labour. It does not do this country any credit to have one of the worst strike records of all the western industrial nations. Quite frankly, the figures are appalling. If you think that I use language that is too strong, you should go to Europe and listen to both labour and management describe our disgraceful strike record. You should go to Germany where trade union members will say, as they have said to me, how can you have a country that has all the resources that yours has, that has people who have, relatively speaking, a very high degree of education, that has obviously people of initiative and competence, and yet so mismanage things, all of you, that you have slipped into a situation of being forced to impose a control system which, if left on long enough, will be counterproductive and in any event will cause a great deal of social and civil strife. This is what a German trade unionist told me. I had the privilege of meeting some of these people during this recent summer.
The record is appalling and all members of the House know it. We must find some way to do something about it. I should like to quote from a speech the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) made on May 25, 1976. He gives government figures which I am sure are accurate. He said:
The number of man days lost in work stoppages has risen rapidly from an average of six million a year over the period 1970 to 1973 to nine million in 1974 and 11 million in 1975.
He went on to say:
The first few months of this year indicate that the record of man days lost may be improving.
That is highly dubious if you look at Mr. Flynn's articles. He has been studying the changing rate in strikes and they may be increasing again.
I want to point out something to all members of the House and especially to my friends in the NDP who sometimes seem to think that the Conservative party has no concern for the 2.2 million people in the CLC as well as the other million organized workers outside the CLC, their wives and families, and another six million Canadians who are in the work force. I want to say to the NDP that we are as aware as they are, and sometimes more so, that these people are Canadians, that they are our neighbours, our friends, our sons and daughters and

I want to read to hon. members a comment made by the former minister of transport, the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand), about the system that we have today. He said:
How is the level of wages established? Is it according to a certain rule of justice, as I heard yesterday? No. It is according to the strength of each party. I have been in that trade all my life. I was involved in certain strikes where the justice of cause was very clear, and we lost. I was involved in others where it was less evident, and we won. Why? Because we were weak in the first place and strong in the second. This is the way disputes are settled. They are not settled according to certain criteria or principles known or accepted by everybody. It is free bargaining.
The problem with that, of course, is that it leaves us in a situation in this country where the strong unions will be able to constantly secure their position and the weaker unions and the unorganized will be left out. It also means that the philosophy in that statement is to be carried on, that you are going to have the collective bargaining system continue without any consideration whatever for the general climate within which individual bargaining is taking place. I think there are 100 affiliated unions in the CLC and of those there are 9,000 local unions. As many hon. members well know, there is an immense number of individual contracts worked out in the country. I might say in fairness that far more are worked out peacefully than with labour-management strife.
But we will have to find some way by which management, labour and government reach some basis of agreement as to where the economy is going, how it is to function effectively, and what are the appropriate shares that any one of these three groups should be able to take from the Canadian economy without jeopardizing the economy as a whole. It is very difficult to disagree with that statement because it should be

accepted as basic common sense. That statement is not misunderstood by trade union leaders in this country. It is misunderstood by some, but there are a good many who understand it perfectly well. One of the things that has happened this year, the most significant thing, I think, in a number of decades of Canadian labour history, has been the CLC manifesto which was declared in the May meeting at Quebec City of the Canadian Labour Congress. Every member in the House should pay a great deal of attention to that manifesto, not only to what is in it but to what is not in it and to why that manifesto was ever enunciated as well as what lies behind it.
Put very simply, the Canadian Labour Congress believed that after the doublecross they received from the federal government on wage and price controls they had to have a closer liaison with the government of the country because it was obvious that whatever their views were they were not being taken into account. Second, they could not trust a government which talked at them but not with them. If hon. members think those words are too strong, they should ask anybody who attended the so-called consensus talks which went on under the aegis of the former minister of finance month after month. During all that time the government never set out to labour what it thought the economy could do, what its own plans for the economy were or what its long term objectives were with respect to employment and industrial strategy.

They did not have any; that is why they did not indicate them. However, as a consequence of that we have a government day after day in the House of Commons retreating from questions by this party, by myself, by members of the NDP and the Social Credit Party with regard to what is happening in the relationship between government and labour in this country.
What did the minister of Labour keep saying? He said that the government was talking and that the former Minister of Finance was having consensus talks. What did the former Minister of Finance say? He said that it would not be appropriate to say what labour was thinking. The fact of the matter is that the government knew perfectly well what labour was thinking. The government was not listening, and in addition to that, during those entire consensus talks it never gave a hint that it was going to double cross labour and bring in the controls which it promised labour in 1974 it would not bring in. One of the problems we have now is that there is not any trust between labour and the government. Unfortunately, that lack of trust is also in other elements of the community. However, if we are going to have a better climate of labour relations, we must have trust. That does not mean that labour is foolish enough or naive enough to think that in all ways at all times every government will agree with it.
Labour is grown up; it is tough and it knows it will not get its own way all the time, but it would rather have a government indicate that it has to put in controls, if that is to be
October 14, 1976

done, rather than a government which indicates that it will never put in controls, that it would not do that to labour or that it would not freeze wages, as the Prime Minister said all during the 1974 campaign, and then double cross labour and do that without warning, despite the fact that consensus talks were being held.
What has been the response of the government since the controls program came in? The response of the government has been, first, to say that it is carrying on some talks with the Canada Labour Council, which was established. That did not last very long because Mr. Morris pulled his people out of that and the Economic Council of Canada. It is true that at the time I criticized labour for pulling out because I did not see that it would do any good. Labour's response was that it was not doing any good to stay there. That is more an indictment of the government than of labour.
So, what is the answer? The answer is found in the proposition that there must be, on a consultative basis, continual rapport, discussion and understanding between employers, labour and government. The CLC manifesto moves in that direction. Unfortunately, it also contains some other things which need some very careful analysis.
Speaking to the Trade Union Congress in Great Britain on September 9 Mr. Morris told his colleagues there about the CLC manifesto, and he said the following, which bears the consideration of every hon. member:
The new body, to be possibly called the Council for Social and Economic Planning, would be created by legislation and would report to Parliament through a Minister. The powers delegated to this Council by Parliament would be carried out by a number of subordinate specialized boards and agencies.
He went on to say the following:
The proposed tripartite body would also have delegated powers to redress the present distribution of income in Canada. The Council's activities in this area would include previewing draft legislation, reviewing current practices, proposing improvements to law and practice, and initiating new programs and projects. The fields of concern would include old age pensions; workmen's compensation; health, maternity, unemployment and other welfare benefits; family allowances . ..
That is an amazing amount of power to propose that parliament delegate to any agency, and the difficulty in this is that it is a delegation which really would remove decision making from the government and approval from parliament. It will be important to persuade trade union leaders that their proposal does go farther than our system can probably accommodate.
This ought to be well known by trade union leaders because certainly their rhetoric-and I am convinced much of their practice-is intensely democratic. One of the difficulties the CLC executive has had in obtaining the power to speak for all its members has been the reluctance of the affiliates to transfer the democratic power they hold within their locals to that executive. Anyone who understands labour relations in this country knows that that is true.
So, it will be incumbent upon us to speak with labour-and hon. members should notice I said speak with, not at-and try to persuade labour leaders that perhaps this proposal goes too far. I think a great many of the rank and file of labour will
The Address-Mr. Fraser
realize that it is not practical to take from parliament that amount of power. If hon. members have any doubt about just how much power is being asked for, I refer again to the speech given by Mr. Morris where he says the following:
We also adopted a policy statement, called Labour's Manifesto for Canada, which determines the general orientation of our movement and calls for the creation of a tripartite decision-making body which would have powers to plan social and economic policy, control private and public investment and supervise national income redistribution.
It is the position of this party that the powers asked for in the CLC manifesto are more than the democratic system can provide and that it would be a great mistake to establish in that kind of an agency. However, it is also recognized that what brought about the CLC manifesto was a determination on the part of a great many people within the trade union movement to play a more significant part in the affairs of their country. This is not new in the trade union movement. It can be found in Europe in almost every country which has a productive economy and a high degree of accord between management and labour.
What is called for is probably a multiparty consultative system which would be established at first on an informal basis in which government, management and labour would meet on a consistent basis to examine what the economy is doing, where it is going and what it will bear. Hopefully, the result of those discussions would be that nobody in this country, whether it be government, management or labour, would be destroying the economy, which is absolutely vital for the future well being of all Canadians.
We have some specific suggestions to make as to what form this body should take. We are convinced that there must be a consultative mechanism which involves labour, management and government. We believe this procedure ought to be followed in each province because we recognize federal and provincial divisions of responsibility. We believe that such an institution can only develop if it is, first of all, truly representative and, secondly, if both labour and management can send to it representatives who can speak for their respective bodies. I might comment that while labour has difficulty in finding representatives who represent all labour because the Canadian Labour Congress does not represent all organized labour and there are another six million Canadians who are not organized at all-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, management does not have any representative group that

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Fraser
speaks for management in this country. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association speaks for some manufacturers, chambers of commerce speak for some businessmen, boards of trade are usually local and confined to their own cities and provinces. As a consequence, when the government wants to speak to business it calls in half a dozen of the so-called leaders of industry, and now John Bullock to represent small business, and thinks it has had a discussion with business in this country. It just is not so. As a consequence, if this institution is to work, both labour and management will have to be able to send representatives who really represent and speak for them. We believe that, on the management side, both large business and independent business must have their own representation. Their views and interests are not always the same. Government and municipal employers must also be represented.
On the labour side, the Canadian Labour Congress is, at the present time, the principal labour association but some adjustment must be made to include the other one million union members and something must be done to recognize unorganized workers and farm workers.
We do not believe at this time that this proposed body ought to receive power delegated to it from parliament. Like anything new, it is too much a departure from the traditional Canadian practice to invest an untried association with what amounts to governmental executive decision-making powers. We believe that there should be recognition that the Canadian Labour Congress does not speak for all labour and big business leaders do not speak for all business. Keeping this in mind, there should be equal one-third representation from labour, management and government.
We believe that such a consultative body will only command public respect and confidence if it is clear that all three groups agree that, despite the differences, they will continue to meet and use their best endeavours to find agreement. Such a body will not function if government, labour or management insists on withdrawing just because there is disagreement. Disagreement must be anticipated; the task must be accepted and it is to find agreement.
There must not be any suggestion that such a body is a substitute for the government of the day or the parliament of the day; if there were such a result it would be the antithesis of our democratic parliamentary system and, not without importance, it would be contrary to all the rhetoric and much of the practice of democratic trade unions in Canada. It is also our belief that long before such an institution is established there must be a series of discussions and the form of organization must be agreed to, subject to modifications from time to time. For the present, we see no need to legislate the formation of such a body because its early success will of necessity depend upon flexibility and in all likelihood in the early stages, constant adjustments.
Mr. Speaker, there is a reason to emphasize the importance of this relationship between government and labour because, as I pointed out, we cannot continue to have a productive economy, hopefully giving more to our people as time goes on and caring for the increased number of Canadians that will be

here, unless there is fundamental agreement and accord on where we are going and what the economy will bear. This is going to require great frankness on the part of government and it is going to require great responsibility on the part of management and great responsibility on the part of labour.
I say to all hon. members-if you want people to act responsibly, give them responsibility, It is about as fundamental a fact in human experience as can be found. The message that is coming to us quite clearly from labour in this country is that despite all the anomalies and at times erratic behaviour, increasing numbers of trade unionists and trade union leaders are asking for responsibility. If this can be achieved, then all the other details of industrial bargaining will have some meaning. But unless there is fundamental accord between the various sectors of the economy on what we can afford to do and what kind of economy we want to have, all the other measures will be patchwork at best.
If there is any doubt that some such consultative process is necessary, I again remind hon. members that the European experience, while in a different environment than ours, clearly indicates that where you have a good economy and a high degree of accord between labour and management, some sort of consultative system like this exists.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that it might be of advantage for this House to hear the words of the former prime minister of Great Britain on this matter. In the British House of Commons on July 7, 1976, Mr. Heath said;
Those countries which have had the greatest success in dealing with their industrial situation are those which, in one way or another, have the closest form of consultation with both sides of industry. Those who have studied this will know that in Japan, Germany, Sweden or even Singapore-in those countries where there is close consultation-there is always the best result from the point of view of industrial production and, incidentally, from the point of view of dealing with inflation.
Mr. Speaker, on this day on which labour has chosen to take an unusual step in Canadian history by calling for and launching a national strike or national day of protest, it is important to look beyond today to see just what we can do in the coming months to repair the damage of the last several years. Fundamental to that is the establishment of a climate of trust within which management and labour can deal with government. It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that before too long this party is going to have an opportunity to establish that climate of trust for the well-being of all Canadians.

It is appropriate on the anniversary of the first enactment of the price and income control program to review the events of the past year, talk about the impact of the controls and of certain events which have occurred, particularly with regard to the so-called day of national protest. I intend to do so in the course of my remarks.
When the government announced the controls program a year ago we said that we would rely on four instruments to recapture economic stability. The first three of these, fiscal and monetary policy and controls on profits and incomes, I shall have occasion to talk about during the course of my remarks. I want to begin by referring to the fourth of the instruments to which we made reference, that is to say, to the approach which would comprise an examination of structural deficiencies in our economy and its institutions.
This afternoon I want, on behalf of my colleagues, to table in this House and release to the public a Government of Canada working paper on the Canadian economy in the post-control period. If we are to act to preserve our long-term interests as individuals and as a nation, we must arrive at as common an understanding as possible of the nature of the prospects and challenges before us.

We suggest that the policy directions set out in this paper be viewed as an agenda for future consultations. We welcome the advice of all Canadians in the modification or the further elaboration of the analysis contained in this paper and the policies it suggests. I would ask that this paper be read with consideration. All will find
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald something here that they disagree with, or that argues against their particular interest. We expect that they will make known that interest. Frankly, we expect that they will do more.
This paper suggests that there are deficiencies in our economy and its institutions that of themselves contribute significantly to inflation. If these factors continue to operate, inflation may well return at intolerable levels once controls are removed.
Continuing inflation will give rise to greater public demands for government intervention to offset the inequities generated by the inflationary process. If governments are to be able to meet social and economic objectives with less rather than more intervention in the economy, inflation must be held to a minimum. I think we must recognize that the Canadian economy may continue to be vulnerable to inflationary forces as we move into the 1980s. This is why there needs to be a wide understanding of the nature of problems and as broad a consensus as possible on measures to correct them.
The international economy will be marked by strong competition for resources and for markets in the 1980s. Continued growth will add to pressures on the prices of foods, energy and mineral resources. The rate of growth of the labour force in Canada will slow in the 1980s, leading to tighter labour markets. Very large investment requirements will put pressure on our capital resources. Competition for financing, equipment and skilled labour will increase, bidding up the prices of all these economic goods.
There are indications that western industrial democracies in general may be entering a period of declining increase in both productivity and growth. Our expectations of rising standards of living will therefore have to keep step with economic performance. These and other challenges will tax our skills and our ability as Canadians to seek the common good of society and co-operate toward its realization.
Hon. members will note in this paper that an essential theme that emerges is the necessity to increase both the reliance on and the effectiveness of the market system as it operates in the Canadian economy. The interplay of dynamic forces that results from an effective market system and has led to continuing economic growth must be encouraged. The role of government policy therefore cannot be to direct and manage the economy in detail. This not only would threaten growth, but could result in a government presence that intrudes too much in the daily lives of Canadians.

It will therefore be necessary to devise means of assisting the market place to serve fully the social goals and aspirations of Canadians. This may require policies to improve the operation of the market economy. Such policies must be developed and managed in a way that allows governments to fulfil their responsibilities with less rather than more direct intervention in the economic system. Such policies must

The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald
provide effective alternatives to increasing public expenditures and expanding public bureaucracy.
In this paper we have indicated a middle role for government. That means that we are looking to the other groups with power in the economy to join with us in the formulation of policy alternatives and to take upon themselves some of the responsibility for the achievement of our society's goals.
This will require a closer degree of consultation than we have undertaken to date, without eroding the powers of parliament and the responsibility parliament vests in government for ultimate decision-making. An approach of this nature could enable us to attain our economic and social goals while maintaining the maximum freedom from interference and freedom of initiative. Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at one o'clock I had indicated to the House the government's approach to the post-controls period, and put before the members a suggested agenda for consultation to deal with the economic problems we now face and will face through into the decade of the eighties.
As I mentioned, this is also an appropriate time, on the first anniversary of the anti-inflation program, to speak as well about that first year and to pose the question, "Where do we stand after the first year of the program?" I suppose that the most direct response, the ultimate measurement by which inflation has always been gauged in this House, is the consumer price index. On that criteria, the year's review gives some ground for optimism.
Statistics for October are, of course, not yet available. In September, the inflation rate in Canada, on a national basis, was 6.5 per cent. Last year, in October, when the anti-inflation program was introduced, it was at the level of 10.6 per cent.
While that 6.5 per cent rate is still higher than is sustainable over an extended period of time, it represents the fourth best inflation performance within the OECD nations and, of course, is a considerable relief from the double-digit inflation we had been experiencing for nearly 18 months prior to October, 1975.
What, then, is behind that general aggregate? Where have the decreases occurred? The most dramatic decrease, of course, has occurred in food. That is partly because of a dramatic drop in the costs of certain meats, because of a drop in the cost of grains and, over the current summer, because of a drop in the price of fresh vegetables.

It may be argued that those declines, welcome as they are to the consumer, owe no particular credit to the anti-inflation program. To the extent that food costs to the consumer are represented by prices at the farm gate, that is correct. However, as we have often heard in this House, as a result of the work of the Food Prices Review Board, and what now seems to be forgotten, is that up to 60 per cent of the cost which the consumer pays for his food arises from the costs of transportation, processing and distribution of food products. It is these additional costs, transportation, processing and distribution, which have been under the control of the anti-inflation program, and those controls have made certain that the lower farm gate costs have been passed on to the consumer.
Looking at other goods excluding food, we have seen an encouraging decline in the rate of increase. It is in the cost of services, most of which are beyond the control of the antiinflation program, where dramatic rates of increase are still occurring. In September this rate of increase was 12.3 per cent.
There are certain price increases which we anticipated would find their way into the consumer price index this month. As part of our over-all energy policy we have to take account of higher prices for oil and natural gas. Because the junior levels of government, particularly municipalities, have had to face higher payments for the services of their employees, there have been higher levels of municipal taxes. In summary, then, the program has been effective. In those parts of the economy where controls have applied, they have been effective to restrain the rate of price increase.
What has happened to wage settlements during this period? First, let us cast our minds back to the bargaining atmosphere in late September and early October, 1975. People are inclined to forget the kind of wage claims that were then being pressed for. For example, 22,000 members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers were looking for an immediate pay increase of 71 per cent and a 30-hour week. Ontario doctors were asking for an increase of between 35 and 40 per cent. Alberta doctors were asking for an increase of 40 per cent. British Columbia bakery workers, meat cutters and retail clerks were demanding immediate increases ranging from 38.6 to 76 per cent. Ontario high school teachers were looking for 43.9 per cent, plus a full cost of living allowance and a $720 lump sum payment. Construction tradesmen in various localities in Ontario demanded increases in wage and fringe benefits ranging between 43 and 96 per cent in a two-year contract.
In other words, let us recall that because of the experience with inflation in the previous 18-month period, there had been these wildly inflated wage claims that were being put forward at the time the controls were put into effect.
What has been happening to compensation increases, wage settlements in particular, in the period of the program? One area of comparison may be made between the average increases in the second quarter of 1976 as reported by Labour Canada, where the rate was down to 13.4 per cent, compared with an average rate of 21.8 per cent in the nine months of 1975 which preceded the introduction of the program. That is
October 14, 1976

a rate which does not yet reflect the impact of all anti-inflation roll-backs. Despite the slowing down of nominal wage increases, there have been significant gains in real earnings, in the order of 3.6 per cent for the last three months, over the same period a year ago. Labour income increased by 16.4 per cent between the first half of 1975 and the corresponding period of 1976. The labour share of the gross national product has been sustained at the record level of 56.6 per cent. Therefore, the working man and woman gained in real terms as a result of the anti-inflation program.
It is true that because of wage roll-backs by the Anti-Inflation Board, exceptional rates of increase going beyond the necessities of inflation have not been permitted. But those who previously had not had an opportunity to catch up with the work force as a whole have been permitted to do so, while others who had favourable settlements before the program have at least been able to hold themselves even with the rate of inflation during the past year and achieved some real gain.
At this point, and in light of those particular figures, one must ask, "Why a national day of protest?" Mr. Speaker, it will be clear from the foregoing that the protest is not related to any real disadvantage that the worker has suffered. The problem with the national day of protest is the leadership of some of the national trade unions, rather than their membership. I am confident, today, that there are many workers who will support the so-called day of protest more out of loyalty to their trade union affiliation than from any real sense of grievance arising from the anti-inflation program.

Mr. Speaker, let me tell the hon. gentleman this. Recently there has been a lot of talk about polls, and I was therefore interested in the following poll that appeared in the October 6 issue of the Toronto Star in which the question was asked, "Is the Canadian Labour Congress acting in a responsible manner in calling for a national day of protest?" A decisive 62 per cent answered no to that question, another 13 per cent said they did not know if the CLC executive was being responsible, and only 25 per cent said yes.
Hon. members opposite say that they represent union members here in this House and that the leadership of the CLC represents union members. What was even more significant about this poll was that 58 per cent of union households said that the CLC leadership was being irresponsible in holding a national day of protest. Another 10 per cent of union households said that they did not know whether the CLC leadership was being responsible or not, and only 32 per cent were prepared to support the leadership of the Canadian Labour Congress.
Indeed, criticism of the CLC leadership has not been confined to the rank and file. We have seen the remarks of Mr. Donald Secord, of the 40,000 member Canadian Brotherhood
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald of Railway, Transport and General Workers, criticizing the approach of labour leadership to negotiations and advocating a greater sense of responsibility in maintaining the stability of our economy.
The CLC have legitimate views to express concerning the Canadian economy, and they have important interests to defend. But a vocal minority within that organization appears to be seeking to build a base from which they can dictate terms to the rest of the Canadian people. They are demanding that certain of the decision-making powers which are entrusted to parliament be delegated to an extra-parliamentary body. While they suggest that this body report to parliament through a minister, they still wish to be able to have power to direct investment into certain channels and to have undefined authority over labour markets and pricing decisions without referring to parliament on specific decisions.
The CLC has today chosen an extra-parliamentary route to make its protest heard or its power felt. It seems to be demonstrating an increasing preference for the extra-parliamentary approach. 1 suggest that as it does so it will find an even further declining response to its methods from the Canadian people. This government is on record as favouring a continuing and increasing dialogue and exchange of views with organized labour. Indeed, we are willing to explore the modalities of increasing and more effective consultations on the economy with labour, business and other groups, as I have already said. But those who seek to use the problems of our economy to challenge the authority of our political institutions will find no encouragement in their objectives from this side of the House at least.
To be balanced, let us take a look at the other side of the equation. What has been the business experience during the period of the program? There is no doubt about the fact that during this period corporate profits have been under a squeeze. In the first half of 1976 they were up only 5.5 per cent from the first half of 1975, and the share of profits in the gross national product has fallen over the period from 11.3 to 10.3 per cent.
The role of the anti-inflation program in the restraint of higher profits has been important. About 100 firms have been required by the board to return to the public excess revenues gained during the first period of the program. A thousand price prenotification cases have been referred to the board and the full details of these particular cases will be laid before the House when the board makes its report, as it is required to do under the statute.
As the House knows, at budget time I announced the intention to introduce some changes to the price and profit rules under the anti-inflation program, and for this purpose draft regulations were put out for consultation with those affected. There was an extensive program of consultation throughout the summer, as a result of which the government has confirmed its intention to remain with the basic elements of the guidelines, namely, holding corporate profits back to 85 per cent of the net profit margin in the base year, but permitting by way of an investment credit additional revenue

October 14, 1976
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald
where there have been productive investments by a particular firm.
There has been a great deal of talk in the business press and by some business leaders alleging that the anti-inflation program is the cause for the relatively low level of business investment during the current fiscal year. There are really three rejoinders to that observation. In the first place, most major business investment does not look for a total pay-out in the first two years during the life of an investment, and hence would be hardly deterred by a temporary program. Secondly, at this stage in the economic cycle, and with a very substantial degree of unutilized capacity still in the economy, it is not surprising that at the moment additional capital investment is not being put in place. But even apart from those two factors in the Canadian economy, cognizance should be taken of the fact that investment as a whole is not strong throughout the developed world.
I should like to refer the House to the conclusions of Business Week. In this regard it observes:
The world's key economies may be exhibiting the outward signs of recovery, but the growth of capital spending-which should be rising with the recovery-is extraordinarily sluggish.
The article goes on:
Capital spending is lagging behind growth in all the big industrial economies. In the U.S., money is again available in the capital markets. But capital spending is making its slowest post-war comeback from recession.
I would just repeat again to business leadership what I have had to say outside the House, namely, that they and their shareholders stand to gain as much from defeating inflation in Canada as anyone of the rest of us. Purely negative opposition to the anti-inflation program, whether by the Canadian Labour Congress or the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, is shortsighted and against their best interests. As we turn into 1977, what all intelligent management should be looking to is the need for additional capacity and the opportunity during that year to initiate projects in favourable economic terms, rather than postponing those kinds of decisions, lest we find ourselves again with spiralling costs of the kind we had in 1973-1974.
As a postscript to this review of the controls program, I recently had the opportunity to meet my counterparts from other nations at the International Monetary Fund meeting in Manila. The primary area of concern among developed countries was the need to control the high rates of inflation being experienced in all but a few of them.
The success we have had in lowering the rate of inflation, limited through it is to date, has caused certain individuals to declare that in their view the time has come to drop the controls program and leave it to the marketplace to bring inflation still lower. They cite the relative slack in current market conditions as being adequate to work against excessive wage and price increases. No one would be happier than I, as Minister of Finance, to be rid of the burden of controls at this time. But I am not convinced that market conditions on their own would be sufficient to lead to a continuation in the decline of inflation. Those who advocate the early termination of

controls have failed to give any reason why, in the absence of the kind of national consensus to which I have referred, the rate of inflation should drop in Canada.
In conclusion, I think we should observe that while, of course, the traditional instruments of fiscal and monetary policy would have been available to control inflation in Canada, by using controls to bring down the rate of inflation we have been able to avoid the massive unemployment that would have been generated had we attempted to achieve the same price target relying solely on those two particular fiscal and monetary instruments.
But controls cannot be a permanent part of our economic system. We still have to rely on continued restraint on fiscal and monetary policy, restraint that has already been in effect this year. We have cut government expenditure and we are committed to holding its increase to no more than the rise in the gross national product. The Bank of Canada, with our full support, has announced new monetary targets for growth in the money supply that will decline with the rate of inflation. We cannot be certain at this time as to the outcome of world inflationary forces in the months to come. But one thing we can decide is that we as Canadians should moderate our own demands on the economy so as to make certain that the inflationary forces are not further revived in this country.
The preference of myself and this government is to achieve that kind of objective by consensus, and it is that consensus we are seeking in the consultations I have referred to, for which the documents I have tabled today are the basis. Until we can arrive at some effective agreement of that kind, and so long as we can be certain that the impact of the program is not creating economic distortions that will work against the interest of the economy as a whole, a controls program of the kind we have put forward, we feel can and must be carried through to effectiveness, and in this we continue to seek the support of the Canadian people and members of this House.
