Mr. Speaker, in the more than 19 years I have served as a member of parliament from the province of Nova Scotia, I have been privileged to speak in the throne speech debate and I therefore welcome the opportunity to comment on the proposals put forth by the government at this time.
I would first like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address, the newly appointed cabinet ministers, as well as those who have been newly appointed as parliamentary secretaries. I look forward to working with them during the balance of this parliament.
If we look carefully over the doors of the Speaker's chamber in the other place we will see a number of inscriptions in Latin. One of these quotes ins from Cicero, and translated it means, "Let reason prevail with me, more than popular opinion". I would recommend that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his governnment give serious thought to the sound reasoning contained in those words. Unfortunately, it would appear, after
October 14, 1976

reading the Prime Minister's statements, that reason no longer prevails among him and his colleagues and, of course, Mr. Gallup has indicated that this administration no longer enjoys the popular support of a vast majority of Canadians.
Apparently, this fact has finally seeped through the vast bureaucratic buffer, built at great public expense, which surrounds the Prime Minister and his cabinet. It has been interesting to the Canadian people to note the Prime Minister's reaction. At first there was disbelief, then frustration, then annoyance over what the Prime Minister construed as the stupidity of many Canadians who, despite an army of bureaucrats, consultants and public relations men, were seemingly unaware of the benefits provided them by this government. "We will soon fix that," said the Prime Minister. "We will take more than $1 million of the taxpayers' money and in this year of restraint we will run some ads in all the newspapers from the Atlantic to the Pacific".
"What shall we say?" asked his supporters. I presume the Prime Minister told them something like this, "Run the ads and say Pierre Trudeau practised his judo while eating his humble pie; he put in his thumb and pulled out a plum and said, 'What a good guy am I' ".
In light of recent political visits to Atlantic Canada and elsewhere in this country, as well as recent events in this splintered cabinet, the Prime Minister may well feel like emulating Dean Martin who goes around singing, "Everybody loves somebody some time; why don't you fall in love with me somehow?" However, the Prime Minister's fall love fest is as divisive as it is expensive.
In fact, one of the most misleading statements recently made by the Prime Minister is reported in the headlines of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of October 4, in which he stated, "Time is running out for the Liberals" and that Canada was in danger of breaking up over bilingualism. That statement reminded me of headlines I read one time when I was in the United Kingdom. They read, "Gales lash British coast-continent is isolated". It was not the continent that was isolated at that time, and it is not Canada that is in danger of breaking up over bilingualism. It is the Liberal ship of state which is in danger of breaking up, not on the rocks of bilingualism but on the shoals of faulty economic policies.
I suggest to you, sir, that it took real experts to make a complete mess of one of the world's richest economies. We insult our friends south of the border with our policies on communications, trade, national defence, finance, and external affairs, to name but a few. Then we wonder why they do not come up to visit us during the tourist season. We neglect our resources, and then we wonder why we are short of such necessities as electrical energy, oil and natural gas. We ignore our customers, and we wonder why they no longer buy our goods which are no longer competitive in world markets or competitive in our own. We define Canada as the thickly-settled areas of Quebec and Ontario, and then we wonder why our national policies almost never work.
I say to you, sir, that this government has honed the art of evasion and delay until it is razor sharp. The government has
The Address-Mr. Crouse
established the survey and the study as the normal substitute for action and decision. Regionalism and bilingualism are nothing more than symptoms of a fed-up feeling by the average Canadian with the central government which is not legislating in the best interests of Canada.
This administration has endeavoured to choke off every effort by the individual citizen or by the people of a region to develop their full potential. Private enterprise has been systematically destroyed, and today we have the absurd situation in this nation of a flight of capital from our country, at a time when our nation is desperately in need of investment capital.
I say to the Prime Minister that his present-day wearing of sackcloth and ashes comes too late to undo the chaos brought about by his blind hopes, his exhortations, his incantations, his studies in depth and his sweeping theories. They have brought about a steady decline in living standards, a steady rise in living costs and a constant sharpening of the cleavage which exists between regions and between interests within a region.
I would remind the Prime Minister and this government that they cannot, by order in council, make everyone wealthy. They cannot legislate prosperity. If this were possible, it would have been done long before any members who are presently sitting in this House were born. The only way Canadians can enjoy a better way of life and a higher standard of living is through increased productivity. This is not only possible but it is absolutely essential in a growing nation like Canada, and it is long past the time that we should get on with the job of increasing our productivity.
The Prime Minister is reported as stating, in Toronto, "The Liberals are out of touch with a large section of the grass roots-especially west of the Manitoba-Ontario border". His recent tours of Atlantic Canada should indicate, even to him, that he is out of touch with the people in our provinces. There is no better way to learn the problems of a region than by at least listening to members of parliament, who collectively represent all of Canada, which I believe is what democracy is all about.
In the time remaining to me, I hope to alert the Prime Minister and his government to some of the problems affecting my province and my constituency, and I hope my suggestions for improving these conditions will receive at least some consideration by this government.
The problems facing Atlantic Canada, and Nova Scotia in particular, are many and varied. It is difficult to classify one as being more important than another, but one of the main problems facing Nova Scotians at present is the high cost of electrical energy and the fact that it is projected shortly to increase by some 65 per cent without any relief in sight from the federal or the provincial governments. It is true that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) recently issued a new "Energy Strategy for Canada", but its broad outlines barely touched the Atlantic provinces and their power potential. After reading his policy, I could not help but feel the minister is obsessed with oil, that he is ready to allow
80001-S

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Crouse
petroleum prices to rise to world market prices, and that he is satisfied to let the people of my area pay increases of some 25 cents a gallon within the next two years.
He mentioned electricity in its nuclear and coal-fired forms, but he steered clear of what 1 believe to be one of the greatest sources of power in Canada, namely, the development of the tides of the Bay of Fundy. On page 103, under the title "Renewable Energy Resources", he states:
The potential for general application of such resources as solar, wind, geothermal, biomass and tidal power has yet to be evaluated properly in a Canadian context.
So much for tidal power, but it was ever thus! Nobody wants Fundy power except the people; therefore it gets no consideration by Ottawa's planners. If the minister knew that a $3 million study had just been undertaken on tidal power, another in a long list of studies, he gave no indication of it. His desire for oil production and conservation left him far afield. 1 therefore feel it necessary this afternoon to remind him that by establishing Fundy power he would save Canada billions of barrels of oil. The output of Fundy tidal power has been estimated at 87 billion kilowatt hours a year. It would take 125 million barrels of oil to equal that production. Ten billion barrels of oil conserved for other uses over 75 years; that is what the minister failed to say.
These are mind-boggling figures, but the experts in tidal power confirm them. In light of present-day needs, to say nothing of future requirements, it is therefore difficult for me to understand why Fundy power still has no priority in federal government policy, and unfortunately there is no indication in the throne speech that action will be taken on this vitally important matter. Evidently the old fears still exist that developments in Atlantic Canada could provide competition for central Canada. There is apparently a belief among the members of this government that a tidal power project would bring the natural north-south lines of economic co-operation closer; that the captive market-which Atlantic Canada has been to central Canada for generations-would begin to burst its bonds. Obviously, this government prefers to see the maritimes and Newfoundland exist as second-class provinces, with their people dependent on its doles and hand-outs, rather than help them move forward to economic and social maturity, which was the promise of confederation.
The Atlantic provinces, and this nation, need Fundy power for a number of reasons. For example, there has been a tremendous rise in the cost of thermal fuels. There is a growing fear of possible thermal and nuclear pollution. There are new techniques which can spread tidal power over to the peak periods in which it is most needed. There is an extensive market south of the border for energy. There is a huge saving of scarce and expensive oil to be gained by a mobile nation. We should be using Fundy tides to produce electricity, and oil to turn the wheels of transportation. There is an opportunity to improve our infrastructure, to correct our chronic unemployment problem, for I say that industry will always move to a location where there is a large and constant source of power.

There are other arguments for Fundy. The need for electrical energy in our area is expected to double within the next eight years, and every source of energy will be required. Fundy's tides can go a long way toward meeting Atlantic Canada's needs. The development of Fundy is too important for interprovincial and federal-provincial bickering. It has to be a political decision, like the decision to build the St. Fawrence Seaway, or the decision to help repay the $2 billion deficit of the Olympics. In fact, the feasibility of tidal power development in the Bay of Fundy was studied and reported upon in 1969 by a board having representation from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the federal government, and the total capital cost of the three sites at that time was listed at $2 billion, which is the same amount as our Olympics deficit and only half the amount of the funds to be set aside by the federal government and by industry this year to take care of unemployment in Canada, a figure which amounts to something like $4 billion.
I say to this House, however, that the development of Fundy tides will not be an expenditure but, rather, an investment which will repay its investors a hundredfold in vast power production, part of which can be sold at a profit and, best of all, in conservation of Canada's vital oil supplies which everyone knows will not last forever.
Let us put our unemployed to work, not next month or next year, but today, building Fundy power plants. Where shall we begin? Feasibility studies show that an installed generating capacity of 8,828 megawatts-and one megawatt equals 1,000 kilowatts-could be obtained if Shepody Bay, Cumberland Basin and Cobequid Bay were all developed to the fullest extent that modern day technology allows.
This massive outfit of power can be placed in perspective when it is equated with the installed generating capacity of each province around the Bay of Fundy which totals some 3,600 megawatts, or less than half the generating capacity of the proposed three sites. However, the studies have only covered three sites, at a proposed cost of $2 billion, which seems to have paralysed this government into inaction.
Their attitude seems to be that if it is too big for them to handle, they will do nothing, or, "If we cannot do the big things, let us not do anything". I submit to this House that there is a fourth site, with the dam already constructed and with control gates looking after the flow of water in and out at every change of tide. This site exists at the causeway between Annapolis Royal and Granville Ferry and there is a sufficient flow of water through this causeway which could, when harnessed to generators, provide electricity to a large part of western Nova Scotia. With very little additional cost, generators could be installed at the present site without interferring with highway traffic, for the causeway could fulfil both functions. An estimated $1 million would provide sufficient generators to at least set up a test plant at this site, and since this government seems to have no difficulty in finding a million dollars to shore up its failing image, I would ask that this amount be made available to the Nova Scotia government
October 14, 1976

immediately toward a test plant on the Annapolis River causeway.
Since Nova Scotia is also considering the construction of its first wood-burning plant for the generation of electricity, which indicates the depth of our need, I would also ask that the federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources assist my province in carrying out a study of all the possible sources of electricity which could be generated on our rivers. 1 believe that the Mersey River, for example, in Queens County, could provide more electricity for our area, and the beautiful falls at Milton are, in effect, at present wasted energy. At one time electricity generated from a power dam on the Petite Riviere looked after the electricity needs of Bridgewater. Another power dam at Mahone Bay looked after that town's electricity needs along with Lunenberg. In light of Nova Scotia's soaring electricity costs, I believe we must immediately examine the possibility of harnessing the power available to us on all our rivers, power which will not materially escalate in cost once it is developed and which will not use up our non-renewable reserves of coal and oil. Let us get on with this job immediately.
I have dealt with this issue at some length due to its importance in Atlantic Canada, as well as the fact that the increased energy cost is having a marked effect on another very important problem in our area, namely, transportation. The former minister of transport described the problem very well, if not in a very complimentary way to himself, when he said that transport is in a mess. I agree with his assessment. Today it is in a mess that has reached crisis proportions.
I am glad that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is here, because I intend to deal rather extensively with the problems that are faced by his department. Part of the present problem is brought about by the fact that the railroads, which should provide a national service to all parts of the country at equal cost, are in effect providing a regional service at competitive cost only in the heavily-settled areas of Canada while being required by this government to provide service in Atlantic Canada, for example, on a user pay basis. This concept could put our farmers, our fishermen and fish processors, our lumber producers and other industries out of business.
This is not a cliche or a statement made off the cuff. This fact was made quite evident at the transport hearings in Caledonia, Queens County, on September 14 when transport officials were told that the termination of freight service between Caledonia and New Germany would put two large lumber dealers out of business, directly affecting the employment of 70 people and indirectly affecting the whole community. Because Atlantic Canada is a geographical extremity of our nation, we have a greater need for an efficient transportation system than any other part of the country. In light of increasing costs of air and automobile transportation, we should be taking steps now to improve our railway system. Unfortunately, however, I get the impression that this government since 1968 has had a national policy which has brought
The Address-Mr. Crouse
about a gradual elimination of the passenger rail service, while at the same time forcing up freight rates to the detriment of business in the geographical extremities of Canada.
Our railroads are the only mode of transportation made responsible for all costs, while at the same time they are charged with the responsibility of providing service to areas of the country where alternate forms of transportation do not exist. This places management in a very unfair position, and obviously they cannot carry out these two conflicting duties without being granted federal funds toward capital improvements which would increase efficiency.
Government supporters will undoubtedly ask, "Where will you get the funds?" No one seemed concerned when the government was talking about a new airport for Toronto which would have destroyed valuable farm land, at an estimated total cost of $2 billion. The government spent $157 million for a parking garage at Toronto's terminal two, and $90 million for road improvements to serve Mirabel airport in Quebec, to say nothing of the $440 million which was spent on Mirabel which now is referred to as the greatest white elephant in Canada. The government has on its drawing boards, at a cost of something like $250 million, a plan to provide rapid transit service between Mirabel and Montreal. Where is the user pay concept brought into play when you are talking of making these expenditures, and where do you plan to get this money? Our railroads are still the cheapest means of transporting large numbers of people or heavy loads of freight or machinery over great distances, and they will become more important as fuel costs escalate and fuel is in short supply.
They must be placed in a similar competitive position with other modes of transportation. At present, sufficient funds are not being provided in order to make this possible, and this can only be described as a penny wise and pound foolish policy. The value of our railroads was all too evident only a few months ago when air service was terminated as the result of a strike. The trains were filled with passengers from here to Montreal and reservations to Halifax from Ottawa were impossible to obtain. In my opinion, it is a national folly to let this service deteriorate when it is obviously so important to the well-being of Canadians. It would be interesting to see the response of the travelling public to a new turbo or light, rapid, comfortable train service over tracks from Montreal, through Maine to Saint John, Moncton, Amherst and Halifax. The trip would only take a day, thereby eliminating the need for sleeping accommodation, and it could be provided at an attractive price.
I believe the time has come for a reassessment of our transportation problems and for a new list of spending priorities as they apply to our railroads. Regional as well as national interests must be paramount in any transportation policy. It would also be advisable to consider using electricity as the motive power for our trains. This concept has been adopted with great success throughout Europe for many years. Incidentally, this would be a further use for Fundy power.
After serving for two years as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, I could not help but come to the conclu-
80001 -slA

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Crouse
sion that this government needs a new list of spending priorities. The money for investment which would develop our country and improve our infrastructure is available, but it must be funnelled into the proper channels.
Finally, I wish to deal with some of the fishing problems as they relate to Atlantic Canada. Quite frankly, these problems are many and complex and they are not necessarily related simply to the supply of fish. After attending a seminar at the Nova Scotia Fisheries Exhibition in September, I could not help but come to the conclusion, after listening to fishermen, processors, industry representatives and officials of the Department of Fisheries, that every aspect of this industry, from the ocean to the ship to the processing plant to the wholesaler to the retailer, was in need of attention.
In my view, extending the Canadian territorial limit to 200 miles, as is proposed in the Speech from the Throne, will not by itself restore the industry to health. Rather, this action, although desirable and in fact essential, will only attack one problem among many, namely, that of continued supply. In fact, with both Canada and the United States adopting the 200-mile limit, a new set of problems has arisen. Here I refer to the ownership of Georges Bank, an area claimed by both Canada and the United States and an area that produces a large quantity of our groundfish catch and the bulk of our scallop catch which is one of our most valuable fisheries.
Mr. J. H. Warren, Canadian ambassador to the United States, described the over-all jurisdictional issue in a speech to the Rotary Club of Boston on September 15 as follows:
The new era will involve fresh opportunities for and challenges to our bilateral relationship. We shall be challenged to demonstrate that coastal state management does not exclude effective international co-operation.
Negotiations with the United States over bilateral fisheries relations are expected to be protected and complex, a fact confirmed yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) in response to a question I put to him concerning this thorny problem. A similar problem has arisen with France, since St. Pierre and Miquelon are asserting their right to a corridor extending out to sea some 200 miles either as a free fishing area or as French waters. At present, the Atlantic coast provinces contain more than two-thirds of the people who work in the fishing industries. In these areas, as a general rule, with some minor exceptions in certain areas, the more a community depends on fishing, the lower its average income tends to be.
A major problem for Canada's fisheries, especially in Atlantic Canada, is stock depletion brought about by overfishing. Foreign fleets, especially those of the U.S.S.R., are generally held to be largely responsible for this depletion. Since 1949 the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, ICNAF for short, has set the total allowable catches, or TACs, and allocated quotas to member nations. Clearly, the regulating effort of ICNAF has not succeeded in its purpose of regulating fish stocks in the northwest Atlantic, for many stocks, especially our groundfish stocks, are badly depleted. It is this situation, in light of the failure of successive sessions of

the Law of the Sea conferences, that has brought about the promised unilateral declaration by Canada of a 200-mile limit.
This government, of course, must share some of the blame for the depletion of our stocks. It has dillied and dallied over the years, holding out like a carrot on a stick the promise of doing something for our fisherman. It has been the government's delays over the years in implementing the 200-mile limit which have brought about the present situation, and it will take years for our fish stocks to improve to a point where there will be beneficial improvement in Canadian catches.
One problem which concerns me, as well as the fishermen and processors, is the amount of fish declared surplus to our needs by bureaucrats when negotiating fishing treaties with foreign countries, without an adequate scientific study on which to base these figures. To talk of fish surplus to our needs only indicates the lack of knowledge of the government about Canada's fishing capacity. In fact, the Canadian offshore and inshore fleets presently have the capability of catching the entire allowable catch of all the traditional groundfish stocks, with the exception of the Hamilton Bank cod stock. This is especially true when we keep in mind the reduced total allowable catch which will be necessary in order to rebuild the stocks.
In my view, this is simply another area in which there is inadequate consultation among the federal and provincial governments. There should be discussions and consultations among all provincial fisheries ministers and the federal government before any agreements giving away our fish stocks are signed with foreign nations. Our provincial fisheries ministers are closer to the scene; they are aware of the problems, and their advice and guidance would be most helpful to the government. I submit this type of advice and counsel is more important today than ever before.
I also believe that in order to develop a sound management scheme for our fisheries, consideration should be given to such factors as the time of the year when fish can be most efficiently caught, and here the fishermen's knowledge should be utilized. Consideration should also be given to the seasonal variations in the quality of fish, as well as other biological factors relating to the spawning period. We cannot continue in our old ways and habits if we are serious in our intention to rebuild our fisheries resources, and this applies to all ships licensed to fish on our banks, whether they be Canadian or ships of other nations.
In conclusion, in order to clear up our difficulties with the United States in the Georges Bank area, as well as in other areas, we should establish, after consultation, a joint management fisheries commission to manage fish stocks in all Cana-da-U.S. boundary areas. These suggestions will not by any means solve all our fisheries problems, but unless the 200-mile limit, when established, brings greater economic benefit to all Canadian fishermen, the whole exercise will be merely a mirage and a delusion. The throne speech barely mentions Canadian fishermen, and in light of the lack of leadership
October 14, 1976

given by this government on many of the problems I have outlined, I welcome the opportunity to support my leader's motion of no confidence in this administration.

We opposed the anti-inflation program of the government in 1975 because we said, as the Prime Minister has said, that inflation could not be dealt with by wage controls, that price controls would not work and that the program would not be equitable. The events of the last year have demonstrated the validity of the arguments we used in opposing the program.
We have never opposed a genuine incomes policy. A party like ours, which believes in democratic socialism and which works in the same spirit as the social democratic government of West Germany and as the socialist government of Sweden did for more than 40 years-

speechtext:
-did not oppose, and does not oppose a genuine incomes policy which would treat all Canadian citizens fairly, which would not discriminate against the poor and benefit the rich, as the present program does. Let me give just a few illustrations of what I mean when I say that. In the constituency of St. Boniface, which is represented by my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), the large hospital there recently concluded an agreement with its workers which provided for a 16 per cent increase. The lowest rate for unskilled workers at that hospital was the magnificent sum of $3.06 per hour. That works out to just over 6,000 per year, just barely over the poverty level. What did the AntiInflation Board, helped by the administrator, do? It rolled that increase back to 8 per cent, so that these people, of whom there are hundreds, will in fact live with an income which has been described by the Economic Council and by Senator Croll-certainly no flaming radical-as being in a state of poverty.
The workers in the Cyprus-Anvil mine at Faro, in the Yukon, about whom the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) spoke this morning, have been on strike for months despite the fact that they reached agreement with their company, because of the stupidity of the Anti-Inflation Board and the administrator in not facing up to the reality that unless the workers get that increase they will not stay in the Yukon, they will move	to Sudbury,	to Thompson	or to Sault Ste.Marie. Within	a year that	mine	will be	virtually closedbecause nobody	will want to	work	there at	the rates of paywhich the AIB	has imposed.	That	is what	has happened to
ordinary workers as a result of the program.
Let us look at the other end, at how the government and the AIB has dealt with people in the upper income brackets. I am sorry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is not here. The hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) asked about the premier of Manitoba. Let me tell him something about the premier of Manitoba. He really believes in an incomes policy. He was naive enough to believe that this
October 14, 1976

The Address-Mr. Orlikow
Liberal government meant business. When it said that the increase which any individual could get last year would range from a minimum of $600 to a maximum of $2,400, the premier was naive enough, or foolish enough-whatever term you want to use-to believe that the government meant it and that it would apply to all Manitoban citizens, including the doctors.
But what happened when he tried to get the Anti-Inflation Board and the Minister of Finance to put that into operation? The premier of Manitoba believed that doctors are no better and no worse than the other citizens of Manitoba and that they should have to live under the same rules. Suddenly the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board and the Minister of Finance disappeared from the scene and the premier of Manitoba received' absolutely no co-operation. Indeed, he received opposition from the Liberal government and its stooge bureaucrats on the Anti-Inflation Board.
How can the government expect workers like the hospital workers in Winnipeg or Toronto, or the many other workers who are living on poor incomes, to believe it is serious, when they can pick up a recent issue of the Financial Times that indicates the incomes or salaries some of the senior officials of corporations in Canada are earning? Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the only reason we have this information is that tax laws in the United States require that it be filed by companies whose stocks are traded on the American market.
Let us look at how hard done by some of the senior corporate executives are in this country. Last year, the income of the chief executive officer of Alcan Aluminium Ltd. was $235,000; the chief executive officer of Carling O'Keefe Ltd. was $164,000; the chief executive officer of Imperial Oil Ltd., one of those corporations which is crying that unless it gets better tax breaks it cannot continue to look for oil in this country, was $234,000.

speechtext:
That is the kind of situation which exists, Mr. Speaker. It is no wonder that people in Canada simply do not believe that this program is working or that it is fair.
Let us look at the profits some corporations made in the last year. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have said that the controls program put limits on corporations and they would have to make sacrifices like everybody else in this country. Let me put a few examples on the record. Cadillac Fairview Corp. Ltd.'s profits went from $13 million to almost S16V5 million, an increase of 26.4 per cent. The Toronto Star, a great supporter of the government and a great supporter of the anti-inflation program for everybody but itself, went from just over $7 million to $9 million in 1976, an increase of 25 per cent. Of course, the Toronto Star likes having an increase of

25 per cent for itself, and it wants the government to see that its employees do not get a fair share of that increased profit.
Bell Canada, a company which has distinguished itself by asking for rate increases every year since I came to Ottawa as a member of parliament, saw its profits go from $114 million in 1975 to $148 million in 1976, an increase of 30 per cent in this year of controls.
Mr. Speaker, the controls program is not working. Despite what the Minister of Finance has said today, every poll taken shows conclusively that the public, by a large majority, believes it is not working and that it is being applied unfairly. The minister made a great deal of the fact that the consumer price index showed an increase of only 6Vi per cent for the last year. But he ignored some very important facts and glided over some others. He admitted that to a large extent the reduction in the increasing rate of the cost of living is due to the fact that the cost of food has decreased. It has gone down despite the fact that food production is specifically omitted from those fields in which the Anti-Inflation Board can apply controls. It has gone down as a result of very good weather on the North American continent we have had bumper crops and this has led to reductions in the price of beef, pork and vegetables.
If you exclude food, you find some very interesting facts. The cost of housing went up by 11.2 per cent last year. That is not surprising when one realizes that interest rates on mortgages are at an all-time high and there is a tremendous shortage of housing. We are doing little to meet the needs of people in the lower and middle income brackets for housing. The cost of operating a house has gone up by 11.2 per cent. The cost of fuel and utilities went up by 20.4 per cent last year.
Those costs are just beginning to go up, because when we talk about an increase of 6.5 per cent for September-the figure which was announced a few days ago-we know, and the minister knows, I am sure, better than most members of parliament, that this is the first time the increase in the price of fuel has been calculated. The minister knows that by November the full increase which was permitted some weeks ago will show up, and he knows that the government has authorized another increase in the price of fuel in January.
The price of utilities has gone up. The Ontario Energy Board has recommended an increase in hydro rates for the coming year of 30 per cent. That is not the only reason the figure only shows 6V2 per cent. The minister knows, or should know, that the increase in municipal taxes shows up in the cost of living figures only one a year, and the month it is taken into account is November. There has been a very sharp increase in municipal taxes in every city in Canada.
There is another important factor which is not shown at all in the consumer price index. That is the cost of health insurance. The reason it is not shown is that in every province the financing of health insurance is done in a different way. In some provinces it is done through premiums and in others it is paid for out of general tax revenue. That is how it is done in Manitoba. In the three largest provinces, British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, health insurance premiums doubled in
October 14, 1976

the last year. I speak from memory, but I believe it has added in the neighbourhood of $100 or more to the cost of living for every family in those three provinces. That figure does not show up at all in the cost of living figures.
I say the cost of living increase for the year, by January or February, 1977, will not be the 6I/2 per cent about which the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister were able to crow yesterday and today, but will in fact be in the neighbourhood of 8'/2 per cent. Indeed, although the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister crow about a 6.5 per cent increase in the last year, the fact is that if one excludes food prices, the increase from September, 1975, to September 1976, was 9.3 per cent, compared with about 10.5 per cent for the same period in the preceding year. To say the least, gains have been minimal.
A good deal has been made today and in past months about the hostility of the labour movement, of trade unions, to the anti-inflation program and the controls program. For some time the labour movement was alone among the interested groups of this country in opposing the controls program implemented by the Fiberal government. It is interesting to note that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which originally supported the anti-inflation program, has in the last few weeks opposed that program. This country has been governed by Liberal governments since 1963, and by the government led by our present Prime Minister since 1968. Why is the business community now opposed to the anti-inflation program? The reason is obvious: business is having it tough. It claims that this government is making it almost impossible for business to survive.
Let me read two paragraphs from a speech made by a former Liberal cabinet minister who is now a professor at McGill University, Eric Kierans. About a month ago he was addressing the Conference Board of Canada in Montreal and he told the board that business had never had it so good in this country. Fie gave two examples. I quote his first example:
The Royal Bank of Canada was founded-in 1870 and by 1970, 100 years later, had accumulated $11.4 billion in assets. Five years later, i.e., 1975, these assets had risen to $25.2 billion, an increase of $ 13.8 billion or far more than the accumulation of the previous century.
I quote his second example as follows:
The CPR was chartered in 1881 and had accumulated $2.3 billion in assets by 1970. Five years later, and after a consolidation of accounts, the CPR has assets of $6.2 billion. If the CPR is now looking south, it may be because of its size and finds no new worlds to conquer in Canada but not because Trudeau is a socialist who has prevented them from growing.
Why does the business community now oppose the controls program? It is not hard to see why, if one reads business magazines and newspapers. The government promised business that the Anti-Inflation Board would not create a new layer of bureaucracy. Although I have no precise figures in front of me, I knew we were told that the Anti-Inflation Board could do its work with fewer than 500 employees. I have not seen the most recent figures, but I am certain that the board now employs more than 1,000.
The Address-Mr. Orlikow
Further, it was said that the board would not interfere in the day to day decisions of business organizations. The facts are clear. Now decisions are not being made. Workers and companies find they must wait months, sometimes six months or more, for decisions cortcerning agreements concluded with regard to wages. Companies find that the rules are complicated, cumbersome and changing all the time. Instead of using their time to improve business, increase productivity and find new markets, business leaders must spend more time filling in forms and meeting the demands of the Anti-Inflation Board. The current issue of the Financial Times devotes a full page to the woes of business leaders. Apparently, when the program began middle management was given the responsibility for dealing with the Anti-Inflation Board; now business leaders themselves find it necessary to deal with the board. That is how they spend their time.
The business communities of West Germany, where a socialist democratic government is in power, and of Sweden, where a socialist democratic government has been in power for more than 40 years, can communicate better with their governments than can the business community in Canada. The reason has nothing to do with the philosophies of those foreign governments which espouse philosophies similar to those of the NDP. The reason is simple. In the two countries alluded to, where the social democrats are or were in power, and in Sweden they were in power for more than 40 years, business has to pay its fair share of the cost of operating the country; but business also knows the rules of the game, knows what it can do and what it can invest. This country's business community has turned against the anti-inflation program because it does not know how to operate under the new bureaucracy and the new regulations with which this government has saddled the country. They are not working.
1 now come to one of the main reasons for the NDP's opposition to the whole concept of the anti-inflation program. It made no sense to us to dampen the expectations of the people of this country, given present circumstances. It made no sense to say to people of this country who wanted houses, "Well, there just isn't enough money: We cannot build them for you this year, next year or the year after." It made no sense to say to people who wanted a television set, "We can't build enough television sets," or to people in city cores who wanted old schools torn down and their children educated in modern, middle class schools like the ones built in the suburbs, "We can't build new schools; there isn't enough money." It made no sense to say this one year ago or two years ago.
Mr. Speaker, in recent times more than 7 per cent of this country's people have been unemployed. For 17 months we have had greater than 7 per cent unemployment. For months and months more than 700,000 people have been out of work. Given this government's policies, policies which it obviously intends to continue, it is very likely that more than 8 per cent of our work force will be unemployed this coming winter in January and February, 1977. Close to a million people in this country will be unemployed.

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Orlikow
1, as a member from Manitoba where between 18,000 and 20,000 people were unemployed in recent months, or about 4.5 per cent of the work force, find it hard to understand why some hon. members are not more concerned about unemployment. For instance, the newly appointed Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) represents a constituency in Newfoundland where unemployment is running at almost 15 per cent. Nova Scotia is suffering from double-digit unemployment, at about 11 per cent. Unemployment in New Brunswick is running at about 12 per cent, and in Quebec at over 9 per cent. In Quebec, in August of this year, 234,000 were unemployed. The September figures, which were released several days ago, are even higher.
However, members representing those provinces do not seem at all concerned. Do they believe, as do some well paid media people and tenure professors in our universities, that many people do not want to work? Do they believe that unemployed wives are not really unemployed because their husbands are working, despite the fact that the only way they can buy a home and make mortgage payments is if both husband and wife work? Is that what they believe? We do not think so. We in this party believe that we can have full employment. We do not believe that except for the United States Canada must have the highest rate of unemployment of any industrialized western country. We are not alone in our belief that Canada can have full employment.
Senator Hubert Humphrey, who has had long experience as a United States senator and vice-president since 1948, introduced into the United States Senate a bill entitled the llurn-phrey-Hawkins bill. The objectives of that bill have been endorsed by the Democratic presidential candidate, Jimmy Carter. We believe, as Senator Humphrey believes with regard to the United States, that we can and should have full employment. It is the responsibility of the Canadian government to ensure that this is the case.
The record proves conclusively that the Liberal government does not believe that full employment is either possible or important. We in this party are prepared to make a national commitment to full employment. This should be done through legislation. A bill should be introduced setting out clearly and unequivocally a specific timetable for achieving full employment in this country.
We in this party propose that unemployment be reduced to 5 per cent nationally within one year, and to 3 per cent within two years. This can be achieved in Canada in the same way that Senator Humphrey believes it can be achieved in the United States. The Liberal government will not do that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate on the Speech from the Throne. 1 believe very strongly that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has set before us a great challenge, one which the Canadian people might have expected and in all probability wanted. I will divide my speech into two sections. First, 1 wish to point out some of the specifics 1 see in the Speech from the Throne. Second, I want to indicate the inspirational way in which I feel it can have an effect on the Canadian people.
Before the Speech from the Throne 1 wrote to many of my constituents. 1 circulated among many people I know in business, labour unions and professional people and suggested that they write indicating to me what they, as Canadians, would like to see in the Speech from the Throne. I am pleased to say that these Canadians, being as responsible as ever, took the time to do that. Some sent a very short note. Some older people replied in plain ink on scribbling paper. Others with secretaries made four, five and six-page replies. They indicated what they would like to see in the Speech from the Throne. In looking over the speech, I discovered that it deals with the kinds of things they wrote to me about, indicating a response to the Canadian people.
A paramount issue in my constituency is national unity. Most people who wrote said that we need better understanding among French and English-speaking Canadians, but we must achieve formal constitutional independence and increase the effectiveness of training in both official languages in the shod systems across Canada. Those are three paramount thoughts on national unity in my constituency. They have been reflected in the Speech from the Throne.
My constituents wrote to me about equality of opportunity. They talked of a reduction of inflation, creating employment opportunities, practicing fiscal restraint, reducing growth in the public service, transferring some government activities to the private sector and, to increase trade, that we modify our industrial assistance programs. The poeple who wrote to me are ordinary citizens, not paid members of parliament. However, they said many things that were said in the Speech from the Throne.
They asked that we improve financial assistance to small business. In many cases when people talk about small business, they refer only to capital expenditure. Many small businessmen get loans from industrial banks, provincial governments or their own banks for capital expenditure. However, they often find they do not have the funds with which to purchase
October 14, 1976

the ingredients for the new products necessary to fill the orders they receive. They do not have the funds for ongoing expenditures. This is true of many small businesses in Canada. In the fro?.en food business, many small businesses have difficulty fulfilling contracts because they are unable to buy the necessary ingredients. In addition, it has been requested that the amount of paperwork to be completed by small businesses be reduced. For example, a small business with six employees might require the services of one or two employees just to complete government forms.
With regard to unemployment, my constituents wrote that there should be year-round job creation. They do not believe that the work ethic is dead. They do not accept the fact that Canadians are lazy. Often it is businesses, companies and others who utilize unemployment insurance for their own benefit, laying off people in order to achieve new methods.

speechtext: Did you like the speech?

speechtext: Is there such a thing?

speechtext:
Sometimes a speech like this is the vehicle for the expression of the opinion of the Canadian people, and we have a Prime Minister who is becoming very expert in reflecting the opinion of the people.
So far as immigration is concerned, they are asking for some amendments that will further the cause of family reunification. We are all aware of sad cases, yet one of the things that Canadians still continue to ask is whether we are going to assist in the reunification of families. We have always done this, and they want to know whether we are going to continue to do it. Canadians have also indicated their concern for a balance to be struck between immigration and employment opportunities.
1 could go on for pages talking about reflections on the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker. In the field of labour-management relations people are asking about collective bargaining centres, about a greater rate of participation by plant workers, expanded labour education programs, a voluntary code of fair practices, a national institute to improve quality of life in the workplace, and establishing an industrial safety and health centre to identify and remove hazards. These are things that the people want this parliament to do. 1 do not suggest for a moment that the opposition parties will not, in their view, play a very strong role in the legislation that will finally come forward from the Speech from the Throne. Their amendments and suggestions, if for the good of the Canadian people, will
The Address-Mr. MacFarlane certainly do much to mould the policies put forward by the government in the Speech from the Throne.
As for competitions policy, we should strengthen laws for mergers and monopolies and give protection against unfair freight rates. In the field of energy we should increase research and exploration. Other items include social policy, settling the land claims of our native peoples, increasing federal support for amateur sport, family law, external affairs, individual freedom and the role of government. These are all subjects about which ordinary Canadians have written in their letters.
One area where I might be critical is amateur sport. The government has indicated that there will be increased federal support. I will always say that this is not enough, that the support does not go far enough. 1 shall probably never be truly satisfied until we have a minister of sport. 1 do not accept a ministry of state for fitness and amateur sport, but at least this does provide a good plateau from which to start. We can then go forward up the ladder and do things properly in the long term. Those are the matters of substance in the Speech from the Throne.
I have often thought, as I have looked at this great country of ours, at this brave new world, at this Canada, that there must be an unusual and great destiny for us. Indeed, when I saw many of our youth fight in the last great conflicts for Canada, World War II and the Korean war, fighting for what they believed to be the cause of our free society, I thought that at some point we would harness all our human resources and move on to our destiny, which was to bring a new light and a new attitude to all the world.
South of us were the lands where the Statue of Liberty beckoned. These were the lands where they said, "Give us your poor, your hungry, your tired". These were the lands which for so long held hope for a tired, weary world. I remembered, in another generation, how my father had gone to fight the war to end wars, and how he had been so maimed. Lie came through it and brought a family through that terrible depression. 1 remembered living as a family of five in two rooms, and yet I once again remembered how my brother went to the army and my sister to the navy, I myself to the air force, and came through a second great conflict. My hope continually was that this present youth, this present generation, would really not go to war and therefore would end war where my father had failed, where I had failed and my brother and sister had failed.
This must be the destiny of Canada, I thought. Surely this new world had a destiny to bring to the entire universe as we went to the moon and looked back at the earth, a feeling of hope, a feeling of greatness for the future. To my surprise, it seemed as though a destiny had been broken off, not just interrupted but broken off. It seemed as though we had become involved in wars which some people said were none of our business.
It seems as though we had lived in a land of luxury and were no longer interested in other human beings. We had become self-satisfied and we ourselves were all that counted in this tired world. We were taking back our invitation to the poor
70

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. MacFarlane and the hungry to come and bring their tiredness and tribulations with them. The Statue of Liberty had closed its eyes. North America had shut its voice. We might have even shut our ears. It seemed that the entire country was in an internal turmoil. Canadians looked askance at Canadians. New Canadians were looked upon as different. There was talk of separation both east and west. Loud voices spoke out representing each of the founding races and threatened to be unreconciled. It was even evidenced by the fact that racial tension began to rip through our neighbour to the south.
In parts of Canada, new Canadians were looked at as not of our stock. It seemed that we were not in search of a destiny at all, but we wanted to mark time and enjoy the good things that we have for ourselves and we would never share them with anyone else.
In the midst of all this, great problems of corruption were alluded to in government. There seemed to be a lack of moral fibre in our leaders. There was a complete loss of hope in this generation. It seemed as though everyone was out to get what they wanted for themselves. It seemed that destiny was involved in survival today and there was no bright hope in the future.
How could this selfish, self-centred, non-sacrificing community fulfil its destiny to leave the world a bright new future? Our destiny was gone. If we were destined for anything, it was to wallow in the fields of mediocrity and in the valley of sloth. If we were in charge of our own destiny, then our destiny was not to clean the pool but to pollute the pool, the earth, the air, and even the minds of those around us. We had not merely lost our path on the road. We had not merely taken the low road or mistakenly meandered through the fields. We had lost our destiny.
Somewhat bewildered, I stood as though all alone on a mountain top and I could hear voices. Some were very old voices and they spoke of when the days were hard and difficult during the days of the depression, the tragedies of wars. These were pruning days. They had come through these days together, although having faced great tragedies, having lived together, worked together and accomplished something for the future. These older voices said, "You can't lose your destiny. There is a future for you. Look to the new generation". Then I heard many other young voices. These young voices kept talking of how they would gather with the youth of the world. They would gather with the youth across the land. They would unite in love and security. They would bring to society a brave new world.
As I heard these two voices, I heard a clamour which almost drowned them out, and this was the clamour of a third group. They had gone to the best schools, had lived the rich, affluent life. They were the ones who had everything given to them on a silver platter because their parents, having been through so much pain, had said that their children must live better. These were the ones who said that the past was wicked, the future was rotten, let us live for today.
It was in this simple moment, on top of that one hill, hearing those three voices, that I understood the problem we faced on
[Mr. MacFarlane.)
this continent. We were facing the death of a generation. We were facing a clawing, clinging, screaming people who knew they were going, a materialistic group who had no hopes for the future. This middle generation could see only itself and really resented the voice of the grandparents of the past who could talk so joyfully about their hardships. They really resented unknowing youth who talked as though there would be a bright new dawn.
For them, life was measured in pennies and dollars, cars and television sets and all of the materialistic things and objects on which you can put your hands and view and taste, touch and feel. There was no imagination left-the imagination that was so vivid in the stories told by old grandmothers, the imagination that was so vivid in the young boy or girl who thought that he or she might be a pilot, or a fireman, or a nurse, or a doctor, or a missionary.
This society that was dying was cynical. But, you know, the great chance was there. Joined with the youth and the aged, some of this society, you and me, may pull ourselves out from this dying generation. We do not have to sit on the Titanic and slide into the ocean ahead of time to meet it, or just go down with a gurgle.
We have a chance to pick ourselves up and reach for the stars. We have a chance for a second destiny, and that second destiny will be made by the volunteers, the ordinary citizens of Canada. It will not be made by the highly paid employees. It will not be made by the experts. It will not be made by the academics or by all of the researchers or all of the social workers or by all of the greatest of management experts in the world. It will be made by the ordinary citizens from all walks of life. Businessmen, athletes, artists, dancers and corporation owners will give of their own talents, one to the other. We believe our export will be the export of attitude; that our most important resource in this part of the world is human resource and our youth.
We will indeed achieve our second destiny, and our second destiny is a bright new world. Our second destiny is not a city paved with gold. Our second destiny is not all of honey and flowing fields of wheat. Our second destiny is somewhat a drawing in of the belt. Our second destiny is a commitment to be concerned about all others, regardless of their race, colour or creed. Our second destiny means that we will be willing and joyful to sacrifice in order to help others. Our second destiny is no mere ride over the river Styx to the valley of death. Our second destiny surmounts even death. This generation, those of us who will join the youth of the future, will indeed prove, "It's coming yet, and yet shall be that man to man shall brother be".
Service clubs, fraternal organizations, churches and institutions and cities and countries, with this new wave of nationalism will exhibit not our differences but will exhibit what we bring to the table: our talents from Canada, our talents from the old country, brought together not in a melting-pot but in a grand mosaic, a grand stained-glass window which shouts out
October 14, 1976

our destiny. It is our hope for the disenfranchised and our hope for the world. Our destiny is indeed a road that climbs up until it disappears in the light at the end of the tunnel.
Destiny is in the doing. Those who stood side by side and saw their comrades slain in battle in the cause of a new world will join us. Those who survived the great depression have empathy for the poor of Canada and the poor of the world. The challenge of our youth is not once more to be cannon fodder. Elowever, like the noble ones who came before them, their sacrifices will be great. Let us join with them in the doing. We are on the verge of a new generation. We are witnessing the death of one. Let us toss off the tentacles of the materialistic past. Let us move together to a bright new world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is going to be a very difficult act to follow, as I see that the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) has just emptied the press gallery. This is the first time that has happened since 1 have been here.
I should like to start by congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. In supporting the government's programs, those two backbenchers displayed what 1 think is an inordinate amount of courage and fortitude. My intention is not to give a wide-ranging speech on the economic ills of the country, as that certainly will be left to other hon. members. 1 would like to give a brief rundown or expose of my thinking about the case for a long-term food policy for Canada and outline some of the reasons we should have such a policy and what has happened in agriculture over the past decade.
My interest in agriculture is certainly both political and practical; political since my constituency is totally agricultural and practical in that I am proud to say 1 am a practicing agricultural producer in Manitoba. I believe the greatest occupation in the world is that of agriculture. To my mind, there is no greater profession than that involved in the raising of food for one's fellow man. Canada has always had what was considered a progressive agriculture, that is, up until the last few years. What 1 would like to do is build a case, as I have mentioned, for a long-term food policy for this country.
It has become increasingly apparent that Canadian agriculture in recent years has gone through a crisis of leadership. As a result, agriculture has been found wanting. Some of the issues which have consumed our farm leaders over the past few years have been egg marketing, dairy quotas, rail line abandonment, feed grain policy, the tinkering about with the beef industry, to name only a few. All of these are essentially negative issues. The strategy each time seems to have been to cut losses rather than to maximize opportunity or try to preserve something that might have made sense decades ago, rather than to sec if they would make sense decades from now.
The leader of this negativism that has spread over Canadian agriculture has been the present minister, and during his term as Minister of Agriculture, Canadian farmers have faced the best opportunities they have ever seen. Such opportunities
The Address-Mr. Murta
usually come to an industry only once in decades, and for Canadian agriculture it has taken over 50 years since it has had the opportunities agriculture has faced in the past three or four years.
One could ask what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has done about these opportunities. I think the very simple answer is that he has made a mess of them. About the only product the Minister of Agriculture seems capable of getting Canadian agriculture geared up to produce is milk powder, and that is about the only major export product Canadian farmers produce that is really not needed in quantities in world markets.
As an example, world grain markets have expanded by about 40 per cent in the last five years, yet the United States has taken about 85 per cent of those expanded markets. There is much evidence of the failure of Canadian agricultural policy in the past decade. As an example, Canadian agricultural productivity has been pitiful. When all resources are taken into account the level of Canadian agricultural productivity from 1972 to 1974 seems the same as ten years ago. No wonder a good portion of the industry is running to hide behind the negative sort of policies we have adopted in this country, policies that have been expounded at great length by the negative Minister of Agriculture.
One can ask whether this can be turned around. That is a fairly legitimate question, the answer to which is, hopefully, that it can be. Certainly, at the present time some of our top economic policy thinkers in the federal government have become aware of the problems related to Canada's approach to farm policy. The unfortunate truth is that this would require a new Minister of Agriculture. The most positive thing the present Minister of Agriculture could do for Canadian farmers is quit. That is unlikely to happen, at least in the foreseeable future, and Canadian agriculture is likely to be adrift and leaderless for some time.
In talking about a long-term national food policy, we must ask ourselves what we should be looking at. I suggest we will have to deal with this very important question in the very near future. It would be wrong to say that no food policy exists in Canada. On the contrary, there are dozens of policies at both levels of government affecting food production, distribution and consumption.
If you want a good example of non-cooperative federalism, it would be hard to beat the array of legislation and regulations affecting the food system in this country. Not only is there a frequent inconsistency of regulation from one jurisdiction to another, but there have been cases where within the same jurisdiction one department's policy has conflicted with that of others. A good example of this can be found in a situation surrounding border control on eggs. It would be interesting to know how the authorities at Industry, Trade and Commerce rationalize their policies with those of the agriculture authorities when it come to Canada-United States trade policies.
80001-6V2

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Murta
Given the propensity for the right hand not knowing what the left hand is up to, no doubt there have been many attempts to provide some over-all structure to governmental activity in the food sector. For example, 1 understand that the federal government formed an interdepartmental committee of senior officials a year ago to deal with food questions. It was established to co-ordinate departmental programs affecting all areas of food. Although this group has doubtless been very busy during the past year or two, there has been no public indication suggesting that this group has seriously engaged in a long-term food policy. It would also be an exaggeration to say that no province has adopted long-term food policies. In Quebec, for example, I understand that the government has set its sights on self-sufficiency in food over the long term.
I have to ask myself how practical that policy will prove to be. It may make sense politically, but it certainly is highly questionable in economic terms. But at least it is a long-term food policy against which the various short-term government measures in that province can be measured. It provides an objective against which the means adopted in particular circumstances to solve a problem can be evaluated. It is precisely the type of clear enunciation of long-term objectives, based on a national consensus, which I think Canada requires.
There are good reasons Canada has not yet managed to develop a long-term food policy, reasons other than obstruction and the negativism of the Minister of Agriculture. First, there is the fact that for several decades food has not been a pressing concern for most Canadians. We have taken very low relative prices to be the normal state of affairs. We ignore the fact that by international, as well as historical standards, Canada has been extraordinarily blessed in its food resources.
Another important factor which has militated against the development of our national food policy, and which will continue to do so, is the array of jurisdiction of authority over the various aspects of the food question. 1 do not believe it would be an exaggeration to say that there are more than 25 separate departments and ministries of government in Canada with regulatory authority over one aspect or another of the food system. This kind of confusion of responsibility remains a major deterrent to the development of a national food policy. In my view, it can only be overcome by firm and statesmanlike leadership at the federal level. Nothing is more basic to society than food. Reflecting this fact, the various elements of Canada's food industry constitute a very large portion of the total national economy.
As a fundamental concern, it is questionable whether we can afford to leave this sector any longer without an over-all direction or framework on which the activities and planning of both government and the private sector can be based. It is questionable because circumstances have been changing. It is evident that when people no longer can count on cheap, abundant food, when instability affects both their stomachs and their pocketbook, there emerge powerful passions and forces in our society which could very well be destructive.
(Mr. Murta.|
At the risk of oversimplifying the problem, existing policies in Canada were generally designed to cope with the problem of food surplus. As time goes on, we seem likely to face a situation of increasing global food scarcity. When the world situation has reached a point at which a country like Brazil decides, as a matter of foreign policy, to increase production of food because of the political influence food will give it in the world council, then circumstances have indeed changed radically from the decades of bulging granaries. When food begins to become a political and even a military weapon, it is indeed time for Canada to disregard the luxury of co-ordinated short-term, ad hoc food policies.
The next question that could be asked would be, what would we be looking at in terms of a national food policy? I am sure the government will be asking this question, because apparently it has no idea what a national food policy should look like. At the national level, I think we should be looking toward an umbrella framework which would provide a consistent orientation to policy-making. It would provide agreed parameters within which discussion affecting food production, distribution and consumption could be taken. The framework for a longterm national food policy should be relatively inflexible in terms of the goals or over-all objectives which it would describe, but it would not otherwise be limited by the means of achieving these goals.
Another important characteristic of a food policy should be that it be practical. It must provide a useful perspective on real problems and offer fairly straightforward guidance, reflecting a national consensus so that it can be adopted by successive governments in any particular region of Canada. Of course, it is easier to describe the characteristic of a long-term national food policy than to actually articulate a policy with those characteristics. The process of articulation will require contribution from as many interested and informed people as possible. It should not be left exclusively to government officials or politicians.
A comprehensive national food policy should address itself to the following concerns: first, output. Canadians must be assured an adequate supply of good quality food. Second, nutrition. The quality of food for all Canadians must be maintained at the present high standards. A national food policy would certainly have to ensure this particular aspect. The national food policy would have to address itself to the most important question of farm income. Without going into any details, adequate incomes to producers will in the future have to be available to those willing to participate in a modern, up to date agricultural industry.
In a comprehensive, long-term national food policy, we must also address ourselves to the problem of Canada's role vis-a-vis the world. We cannot consider our food situation in isolation alone. Thus, our food policy would have to be concerned about our trading relationships and be as aggressive and market oriented as possible. We have already seen, in the case of beef, what can happen if we forget that there are two sides to the case of import controls. Similarly, a long-term food policy would have to articulate Canada's role in alleviating world
October 14, 1976

hunger. Before being able to arrive at any kind of policy conclusion in this area, it would be necessary to attempt to identify exactly what the world food situation is now and what it is likely to be in the near future. With the government's track record, we may see some of the suggestions I have made in a national food policy proposed at some time by the Liberal government. If this is the case, so much the better.
One thing is clear: unless the Minister of Agriculture changes his tactics, he will go down in the history books as one of the most negative ministers of agriculture this country has ever had, and along with the negativism he will leave a legacy of confusion and distrust and a clear record of total lack of any constructive policy.
