speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to pay a special tribute to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada and extend to him my best wishes of good health, because it is our best asset and only when it has somewhat deteriorated do we appreciate it further. I would also like to extend to his wife, his helpmate, my wishes of good health and long life.
I would also like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply, a difficult and unrealistic task that follows parliamentary tradition. It is a long-established custom in our Parliament and in the Canadian legislatures and it is always with some pride that members are called to move and second this motion. This is why I wish to extend to them my warm congratulations.
Mr. Speaker, I am deeply pained that the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada (Mr. Caouette) is not here because he lies in hospital. I am sure that he would have liked to be at present the opening of this second session of the thirtieth Parliament and to take part in its proceedings. Any responsible and sincere individual acknowledges that he is a great Canadian who has worked for the unity of our country while remaining a French-speaking Canadian who has advocated the same ideas in the same terms throughout the country.
So I want to pay him a special tribute and wish him good health so that he can see some day the implementation of an annual guaranteed income through national dividends for everybody and a compensated discount on Canadian products that would be paid through the creation of a new credit from the Bank of Canada, the only democratic financial institution really owned by Canadians, as opposed to the present system that takes the money from the workers through taxes to give it to the less privileged so that someday, if we continue along this line, we shall all be poor.
Mr. Speaker, the first session of the 30th Parliament lasted two years and enabled the government to refrain from announcing its policy sooner. Yet, at the opening of the second session of the 30th Parliament, I thought that in the Speech from the Throne this government would announce several new measures to resolve the many problems faced by Canadians.
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
So it is to fulfill my duties as representative of the people in Parliament that I take part in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The government says that it will continue to fight against inflation but it does not say which means it will use to do it efficiently. The Social Credit Party of Canada would be made responsible for this calamity called inflation if it ever had the opportunity to implement its financial and monetary credit system instead of the present credit-debt system applied and supported by the present government.
In fact, some members of this House and sometimes even the press made unfair judgments concerning the Social Credit Party of Canada without knowing the least thing about its philosophy. 1 even heard recently on the radio in the Quebec area the moderator of a hot line who was ridiculizing this policital trend, this economic philosophy and who admitted at the end of the program that he did not know a thing on the subject. It is unfortunate that people with such a large audience demonstrate so much irresponsibility because either you say the truth or you lie to the people. You cannot do both at the same time. So I urge the management radio stations to assign to those programs people who are responsible. I am not against the fact that our attitudes or ideas are criticized but at least it should be done by knowledgeable people. It is the least we can ask.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, after the government announced its antiinflation measures in October 1975 I declared to the House that once more this government, as the unconscious servant of the big financial institutions, was making the poor bear the burden of inflation in the present credit-debt system. So I declared then that a general wage increase of about 10 per cent would widen even more the gap between the small wage earner and high income people. It was obvious that the injustice would be worsened as a 10 per cent increase for a worker earning $6,000 would give him only $600 more a year whereas those earning an annual salary of $20,000 would get an increase of $2,000 a year which would widen the gap by $1,400 a year.
And that even if the essential needs are the same for all. That is what low income people complain about, those who are not organized, who cannot benefit from regular salary increases, who get only the minimum wage. In my view, this is insufficient for a decent living.
There are thousands of low income people who pay taxes to pay for salary increases of persons who earn much more than they do. That is why I say the gap is widening and discontent growing. That is why we are now experiencing protest throughout the country, even from organizations that benefit-ted from these measures. Nevertheless the low income people who are unable to make representations and demonstrations say so by their silence. They write to their Member of Parliament to complain. I am sure all members receive communications of this kind. These constituents expect us to speak on their behalf on the floor of the House and invite the govern-

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
ment to change its position on that matter and give them a fairer deal.
I think, as it has often been said in the House, that the real solution would be a guaranteed annual income. The government is aware of that question but it makes very little progress on that road. As on other occasions, I am quite afraid that when this measure will be presented the damages will already be too great, it will already be too late, we will be outdistanced by events, and we will not obtain the results that we could get if we acted immediately.
In the Throne Speech, the government reassures us about its intentions as far as the bilingualism policy in Canada is concerned. At last the Liberal party has understood that it will take a long time for Canada to become a bilingual country and the best means to reach that end is to act at the level of the primary and secondary schools, without encroaching upon the provincial responsibilities in the field of education. I sincerely think that the federal government can find a formula that could help the provinces even more, it could grant the fiscal incentives that would enable them to adopt programs for teaching languages, a second language, at the primary level.
I think that that very measure has been adopted in several countries in Europe, countries which are bilingual, and when we go there, as several hon. members may have realized, we often meet people who can speak two, three and sometimes four languages. There is no quarrel about that, it is a recognized fact, an accepted fact and, in these countries, languages do not create any problems. I think that the same thing could be done in Canada.
There are presently some linguistic problems in the field of aviation. Everybody knows about that. We hear more about those problems in the province of Quebec because our Frenchspeaking fellow citizens are directly concerned and they are the first victims. But I do not understand why this useless battle goes on because some claim that people will travel in much safer conditions if only the English language is used in that field.
It is double Dutch to me. How could you have more safety just because English only is spoken in air-ground communications! I cannot believe that we are not intelligent enough to find ways and means to translate faithfully into French all the words used in air-ground communications.
I think this is just an excuse and it seems to me we should show sings of good will throughout Canada, whether we are French-speaking or English-speaking Canadians and try to find a fair and equitable solution not only for the majority but also for the minority.
I was stunned to see ministers resign on this issue. If my information is correct, the resignation of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) yesterday had something to do with bilingualism in Canada. I really cannot understand that. The whole thing reminds me of a fireman. We all know what a fireman is. It is a man who fights fires which are out of control. Some people are proud to be firemen as long as there is no fire to fight, but the moment one breaks out they resign

because they will not fight it. I feel that the best way to be efficient is to stay on the job and try and push one's own ideas without damaging anybody else's cause, but with the conviction of fostering the interests of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the resolution of a municipal council which I received last night. It comes from the City of Montmagny. In this resolution, the city council members state that they support the "Gens de 1'Air" in their efforts to establish French as a useful and practical language in communications. The city council concludes, and I quote:
That it assure ['"Association des gens de 1'Air du Quebec" of its moral support in their fight;
That it authorize the Association to run a subscription and organize a badge selling campaign within the territory of the City of Montmagny for the purpose of obtaining money for their fight;
That a copy of this resolution be sent to the hon. members representing the constituency in the Quebec National Assembly and the House of Commons in Ottawa, to "l'Association des Gens de 1'Air du Quebec", Hangar No. 2, Quebec City Airport.
That is signed by the clerk, Yvon Lemay; the mayor of that municipality is none other than Dr. Cajetan Gauthier whom several of you know for his services to Canada when he was in the Canadian forces. I congratulate the Montmagny city council for having taken position on the matter and I trust the message will be heard in high places so that instead of quarrelling we might get along and finally act like intelligent people and solve the problem.
Mr. Speaker, I was astonished that, in the Speech from the Throne, not one word was spoken about agriculture, as if it were an economic sector of no importance. Yet, as far as Quebec is concerned, it is the very foundation of agriculture, which explains the considerable dissatisfaction expressed by the producers of that province on hearing that, as a result of the dairy policy we know, their income has been cut by 23 per cent as of today. I have here a document I shall not read because it is very long and complicated; I received it yesterday from the dairy producers' union of the south shore, and it is signed by its secretary, Adrien Lavoie. One paragraph reads as follows, and I quote:
Economic situation
The drop in incomes as defined will be $5,350,000, representing 23 per cent.
Considering that 1,200-odd producers in our region will have to face such loss, this will mean for them an average decrease of $4,458 per dairy farm.
Those are official figures which I quote trustfully because usually those people give us very precise information.
Together with the same document I also have here a letter dated September 24, 1976 that was sent to a producer of my region. In this letter, it is said that for five successive remittances, the producer has not received one cent. Each cheque carried the mention "cancelled". I do not know whether it is legal to proceed in such way, I am not qualified to pass judgment but, at any rate, this is called a cheque and no payment whatsoever can be made with it. The producer is unable to pay for his meal account, his hydro and gas bills.
October 14, 1976

Therefore, it is a sad situation but something even worse adds to it. I will quote from the letter, Mr. Speaker:
The Federation of Quebec Industrial Milk Producers have instructed us to deduct from your pay cheque covering the period September 1 to September 15 and the following ones, if applicable, an amount of $1,200.54. This amount represents a deduction for export costs exceeding quotas (penalty) which had not been taken off your pay for the period June 16 to 30, according to the 50 per cent formula as applied to your performance between April 1 and June 30. This 50 per cent formula was cancelled on August 1.
Therefore, for the period I just mentioned alone, June 16 to June 30, this represents $1,200, that is 50 per cent, whereas 100 per cent amounts to $2,400. Consequently this farmer whom I know very well is going to go bankrupt and yet he was among those who were encouraged to remain on their farms because they were employed outside the farm and their wives were running the enterprise with their children. Therefore, he was encouraged to remain on his farm, but for this purpose he had to increase his herd to make his business profitable. So he believed that; he bought cows for a good price, he accepted quotas and he was sure that he would have a normal year. I appreciate the comments you have made, Mr. Speaker. Today, then, I wish to address myself primarily to social policy and particularly to our proposals with respect to the Canada Pension Plan, family allowances,

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo social services and the status of women. While all parties in opposition have tried to shy away from these areas in their comments, probably in recognition that the government is providing solid and popular proposals dealing with these subjects, 1 do want to draw your attention to them. They reflect, directly, this government's feeling that the apparatus of the state exists to do things for people, not to people. Thus, we hold that while we must apply a firm hand where necessary, we must also demonstrate compassion wherever that is appropriate. One place where compassion is vital is in the provision of social services.
In my previous occupation, and indeed in the present one, I have often been brought face to face with what can happen when social services are not available: at one end of the scale, people pushed to extremes of suicide and criminality, and at the other end people weighed down by troubles they have not been able to solve by so-called conventional methods and who are living Thoreau's life of quiet desperation. Somewhere in between lie homes broken by family and financial stresses, people with what society defines as handicaps who are on welfare only because they cannot get transportation to a job, people who desperately need subsidized day-care services, and single-parent families struggling to retain their unity and dignity.
Because I have seen these problems, I take particular pleasure in commenting on the proposed social services act. 1 am very pleased to be the first person to bring to this chamber's attention this very positive outcome of the social security review which was begun by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) some three years ago. There are a number of ways in which this legislation is special. For instance, the very fact that the provision of social services is being considered quite separately from income support legislation is a break with tradition, a forward-looking step which is making Canada the envy of many other countries.
Developing a separate piece of legislation is an important step because it recognizes the fact that those who need services, such as day-care, homemakers' services, crisis intervention services, credit counselling or rehabilitation services, are not only poor people. It reasserts that giving people more money does not magically solve all problems, not even the problems of the poor. It is not enough to be able to pay for a service; the services must first exist.
In effect, this means we are recognizing that social services are needed at one time or another by everyone, although to date not everyone has been able to take advantage of them. Children, regardless of their parents' situation, may need protective services. Their parents, regardless of family income, may need the kinds of services that help bring the family back together again or prevent it from falling apart in the first place. Families with handicapped children need a number of services to make it possible for the child to flourish in a warm family atmosphere without putting impossible strains on family life, exactly the kinds of strains that in the past have forced families to give up their children and place them in institutions. Rehabilitation services which were once reserved

only for people who could work will now be available to people who may not be able to, especially children and older people retired from the work force.
Day-care services are no longer seen as services reserved for the poor; all kinds of people are now using these services. The proposed legislation will make it possible for a much larger number of them to have the whole or a portion of their fees reimbursed. Moreover, day-care is not restricted to children. Many retired people who might otherwise enter an institution will be able to remain in their community and enjoy their retirement a lot more because they will have the opportunity of going to centres where they can meet friends, just relax, or get together to find ways of improving community life not only for themselves but also for others.
Another very important consideration is that the legislation was not conceived in a vacuum. Since this is cost-sharing legislation, thorough consultations were held with the provinces. Moreover, the Minister of National Health and Welfare from the very outset invited submissions from individuals and organizations and received them. The proposed social services legislation from its very conception was a response to the kind of things government was hearing from people. It listened to their concerns and incorporated as many solutions as was feasible into the legislation.
People were saying that no one-not the physically handicapped, not the elderly, not the mentally retarded-no one is so useless that society should automatically put them away in institutions, regardless of how good these may be. Everyone has something to contribute and the right to stand on their own two feet to the extent that that is possible. For the handicapped, this proposal will mean transportation services to get a job or other community activities. It will also mean a range of rehabilitation services which get them ready for a job and make it possible for them to keep it. It will mean living in their own apartment with the help of a visiting attendant or homemaker. It will mean homemaker services for the elderly who want to live in their own home for as long as possible, and for some of them it might mean the provision of badly needed meals on wheels, or a visiting nurse.
We believe that social services are cost-effective. They save tax dollars. There are short-term savings in keeping people off welfare and in the labour market and a number of services do this, including day-care services and rehabilitation services. It is also cheaper in many cases to keep people out of institutions because these have become a very expensive form of care. There are other longer-term savings especially in the prevent type of service. If we can provide children, for example, with services at critical points in their lives, and promote positive personal development, we can be reasonably sure that they will not become dependant adults, dependent on alcohol, drugs, or welfare; they will not be subject to chronic mental illness, or become criminals. For all these reasons, I am sure that many hon. members are looking forward, as I am, to the forthcoming debate on this important legislation.
October 14, 1976

As a result of the recently concluded federal-provincial review of our social security system, several significant amendments have been made to the Canada Pension Plan over the last several years. These amendments improved both coverage and benefits under the plan. For example, the ceiling on pensionable earnings was raised substantially in 1974 and set to increase at 12.5 per cent per year until it catches up to the national average industrial wage level. This means that new Canada Pension Plan benefits payable are much improved. Also, the minimum income levels required in order to obtain access to Canada Pension Plan coverage were reduced in order to expand the scope of the program and extend the protection of the plan to a larger number of Canadians.
In addition, the earnings and retirement tests which applied to Canada Pension Plan retirement pensioners between the ages of 65 and 70 were abolished. This measure ensures that Canada Pension Plan beneficiaries with low pensions are not penalized for trying to improve their incomes by continuing to work. At the same time, the limitation on the adjustment of pensions-in-pay in line with changes to the consumer price index was removed to fully protect pensioners against the erosion of the purchasing power of their pensions.
Another very significant amendment to the Canada Pension Plan was the introduction of equal protection and coverage for male and female contributors and their families. That is, the limitations that had once existed in respect of benefits paid to the survivors of female contributors were removed. This recognized the principle that the earnings of either marriage partner should receive similar protection under the Canada Pension Plan against the contingencies of disability, death and retirement.
The government is now advancing a further improvement to the Canada Pension Plan as part of its continuing program to ensure the plan continues to meet the challenge of this changing world in which we live. These proposed improvements represent one result of several years of study, federal-provincial discussions and dialogue with interested groups and individuals across the nation.
In 1970, the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada recommended that provision be made under the Canada Pension Plan for spouses who work at home. This approach was supported in the reports and recommendations of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Committee, both of which greatly assisted the government in developing these proposals. These groups expressed the need to give recognition to work in the home and to provide financial security under the Canada Pension Plan to a spouse who works at home. As well, a great deal of correspondence was received from individuals and interested groups which indicated that some concrete steps should be taken as soon as possible. These proposals have also been the subject of study and discussion throughout the federal-provincial social security review.
As a result of these consultations, a two-part proposal for amending the Canada Pension Plan is now being advanced.
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo The first part of the proposal would allow the CPP pension credits earned by both spouses during marriage to be split equally between them upon marriage dissolution-that is, upon divorce or annulment.

It means you get half. The second part of the proposal would allow contributors who leave the labour force to raise young children to drop those periods of low or zero earnings from the calculation of their average lifetime earnings in calculating CPP benefits. The hon. member for Scarborough East knows a great deal about this since he was on the committee that helped evolve many of these proposals originally.
The provision to split Canada Pension Plan pension credits upon the dissolution of a marriage is aimed at ensuring, for the "spouse at home", an equal share of an asset that has been accumulated as a result of the efforts of the two partners during the marriage. This provision thus provides a measure of financial security and recognition for the spouse who works at home, and his or her dependants, at a time when Canada Pension Plan protection may be extremely important. The spouse would have immediate financial protection under the Canada Pension Plan against disability, and the children would have protection against the death of their parents. In the longer term, the spouse would be entitled to Canada Pension Plan retirement benefits. This provision is consistent with the view expressed by the federal law reform commission on the economic nature of marital partnership.
The second proposal would allow a contributor who leaves the labour force to raise a family to drop out those months of low or zero earnings from the calculation of average lifetime earnings. This would ensure that any parent who worked at home caring for children under the age of seven would not be penalized for that period during which she or he had low or zero earnings. Consequently, this proposal would protect the potential pension benefits and eligibility acquired by such a parent either before or after the child-bearing period.
Both of the above proposed revisions are endorsed by the government of Quebec which intends to introduce an amending bill to give effect to identical provisions in the Quebec Pension Plan. As a result, the introduction of our proposed amendments at this time will enhance the universality, portability and transferability of social insurance coverage under both the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. That is, Canadians will be largely unaffected by their occupational locale or career mobility because the parallel structures of the two plans will be maintained.
When the government launched its anti-inflation program last fall, it recognized that it had to set an example by curtailing expenditures wherever possible. One of the areas of greatest expenditure is in the income security field. In 197475, federal expenditures on this sector were $ 10V4 billion. However, we also recognized that any cutback in these expenditures would work hardship on the people these programs were designed to help. The family allowance program is the

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Friesen
one welfare program that reaches into all the strata of our society and supplements family incomes without regard to the levels of these incomes.
We concluded that, on balance, a cutback in this program, although it would mean hardship for some families, would cause less disruption of total family income than would a cutback in any other federal welfare program. And by limiting the cutback to the amount of escalation that would otherwise have been provided in 1976, the government sought to limit the impact on family incomes of this anti-inflation measure. The government therefore suspended the indexation of family allowances for 1976; families continued to receive a $22 monthly allowance instead of the $24 allowance that escalation would have provided for. Estimated federal expenditures on this program in 1976 were thus reduced by $220 million.
It should be recalled that in 1972 the allowance rates were $6, $8 and $10 a month, depending on age. In October, 1973, they were raised to $12 as part of the government's program to help people cope with the effects of inflation. The following January, the new family allowance program set the rate at $20 a month, and in 1975 indexation raised it to $22.
However, it is a basic tenet of this government's philosophy that its income security programs should be indexed so that the purchasing power of the various pensions and allowances will not be eroded by rising prices. It would be inconsistent with this philosophy to continue the suspension of family allowance indexation beyond 1976, and therefore indexation will be resumed in January. The exact amount of the increase will not be known until November when the October price index figures are available, but on the basis of current figures I would anticipate family allowances will increase by close to 8!6 per cent in January of next year.
It should be clear, then, Mr. Speaker, that the program of restraint to which our government intends to hold does not imply an end to the improvement of social measures to help those who truly need our help. In places where it is appropriate, we are moving to introduce greater cost efficiency based on the lessons we have learned over the years. In other places we are moving to increase the social justice of our programs. In all cases our ongoing concern will be to provide the very best social security system possible for Canadians at a cost which the nation can afford.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I look forward to bringing information to this House on fitness and amateur sport.

How in the name of logic can he say that prices are climbing more slowly in Canada than in the United States?
I know the Prime Minister is not given to grocery shopping and that the taxpayer pays for all his groceries, but there are many housewives in the lower mainland of British Columbia who would like to take him shopping for a few days-perhaps not by the hand, but rather by the ear. He seems to forget that we are losing $5 million each month because shoppers in the lower mainland of British Columbia travel into Washington State to buy groceries cheaper than they can in Canada. In spite of this the Prime Minister has the unadulterated gall to say prices are climbing less rapidly in Canada than in the United States. I would like him to meet a few of the housewives who do their shopping in British Columbia. He should know, for example, that cookies baked in British Columbia are cheaper in Washington than in B.C.

speechtext:
This is why we are losing markets to the United States and why agricultural products are creating growing inventories in the warehouses of Canadian producers. It will not be long before the farmer in British Columbia is frozen out and our shoppers will be at the mercy of the United States corporate farmers. That is something the Prime Minister is not considering when he makes these bold statements. So much for his credibility regarding those remarks!
Let me make a few comments on the contents of the throne speech which at best can be described as a political survival kit. The Prime Minister is doling out K-rations to his supporters in order that they can stay alive at least until the next election and, hopefully, after it. We, however, hope to lose a few Liberals the next time.
The pablum that was served in that speech was more important in respect of what it did not say than what it did say. For example, the statements regarding the war on the high inflation rate were well taken. This is the number one priority in Canada. While the statements themselves were very innocuous, it is important that we keep that fact in mind. We cannot minimize the anxiety that high unemployment and high inflation create among our people, or the terror they face at the end of each month when they try to pay for their groceries. This war on inflation had better be a real one instead of just shadow boxing.
Even though we might be able to solve all our economic problems in Canada and beat inflation in the very near future, we would still have to face another overriding problem that is perhaps even more serious. 1 refer to the problem resulting from government officials trying to decide for Canadians what kind of people they ought to be, or ought to become. Broadly speaking the problem results from cultural determinism being forced on us. As an example we have the CRTC-and I know there are other such agencies-which have never had to face the electorate, and its members never have to put their jobs on the line. These officials sit on the 14th floor at 100 Metcalfe Street, Ottawa, deciding what Canadians can watch on television and listen to on radio. This is always done in the name of or in the interest of Canadianism.
I would remind hon. members of one thing common to all governments that believe in strict control, as does this government. They always couch their strict controls in the name of and with the cloak of patriotism. They do it for the good of our country and its culture. This means that those who oppose restrictive policies are unpatriotic and un-Canadian.
I remember watching a news broadcast some years ago coming from across the line. That was something I would not have been able to do had the Maple Leaf curtain been properly draped along the 49th parallel. It was a news report by Huntley-Brinkley in which they referred to the parable of a couple of dogs in Germany.
The Address-Mr. Friesen
One dog was from West Germany and the other was from East Germany. The West German dog asked the East German dog why he would want to leave his country. He said he looked well fed and well taken care of, his coat was shiny and he did not appear to be lacking anything. The East German dog said, "I like to bark".
The CRTC wants to tell Canadians how to bark, when to bark, how they ought to listen to the bark, and what the quality of the barking ought to be. But you see the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) is so used to government restrictions that he does not listen any more. He is totally mesmerized by it. The whole Pavlovian theory is working beautifully in his case.
The CRTC bureaucracy with its 700 employees is no longer a regulatory body but rather is a control agency in respect of the Canadian people. It determines what Canadian culture should be. The members of that bureaucracy are the wise ones. No doubt there is a need for supervision, but the main function of the CRTC seems to be to take choices away from the Canadian people. Let me give an illustration by referring to a letter which came to me that was written to the Chairman of the CRTC by someone from Trail. Part of the letter states:
These new FM regulations caused us to lose our local FM station. Small radio stations in rural areas cannot meet these new regulations, and the public does not want its FM listening pleasure ruined. If you are so intent on Canadian FM, how about getting us in Trail some Canadian FM? Your regulations killed our local FM and CBC took over, only to broadcast CBC-AM on our FM station. For years I have been writing trying to get CBC for Trail. Now we have it-but we lost our local Canadian FM in the process. Is this progress?
There you have an example of CRTC brilliance. I should like to refer to a statement made by a very brilliant and outstanding liberal. I have to go back one hundred years to find one, John Stuart Mill, who said:
The cultivation of the active facilities by exercise, diffused through the whole community, is in itself one of the most valuable of national possessions.
There you see is the secret. The community does establish these functions and creates these facilities. We do not need these national bodies to tell us how to live and what kind of people we ought to be. We do need a clear service on the network, but we do not have to be told what to read, what to listen to, and what to watch. It is my firm contention-and I know there are people in this House who agree with me-that it is time for the CRTC to go and that we should have a body which is purely regulatory and not an oppressive control body. That is one area that was omitted from the throne speech. I should like to refer to another.
I refer to page six of the throne speech and read these words:
. .. the government believes most unemployed Canadians would much prefer to secure that income through worth-while work than through public assistance.
I agree, but there is nothing in the throne speech that makes it possible to have the kind of tax relief that would allow private enterprise to expand the way it should if it is to provide these jobs. If Canadians want to work, so do the businessmen. So long as the government continues its oppressive and exces-

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Friesen
sive tax policies, business will be driven out of the country. 1 have a very active but relatively small business in my riding. That business is now diverting some of its activity to the United States. It is tempted to do this because of the tax policies of this government. It is tempted to make its Canadian operation a warehousing operation because it can operate more profitably in the United States. Effectively we have four levels of government all trying to tax the same person. Because the federal government has the over-all tax power it makes sure it gets its tax first.
There is a new television production company operating in Vancouver which some time ago wanted to bring its equipment across from the United States because it could not get that equipment in Canada. It could do so if it would be willing to pay in advance about $100,000 in federal taxes and customs duties. This is a new Canadian company. Meanwhile an American company could have come in and done the same work for $1,500.
All the while the government talks about wanting Canadian business to be totally and purely Canadian. It wants Canadians to own business, but when Canadians have the opportunity preference is given the foreign operators. Now the government talks about a job-creation program. There is no mention of tax relief for business. The government would rather collect all those excessive taxes, recycle them through the government funnels here in Ottawa and give them out in a job-creation program so that more bureaucrats can get a job, rather than let them work there in the private system which they would have been doing in the first place. This is totally unproductive. That is the second point the throne speech fails to discuss.
The third point is that the throne speech says really nothing about criminal law or correctional philosophy. Canadians are crying out for law and order, but they really want more than that. Every totalitarian government in the world can have law and order. What Canadians are desperately crying for is a balanced perspective in criminal law and correction. Their sense of moral and equitable justice, rather than of technical justice, has been completely raped.
Those of us who live in British Columbia and represent the people there have very fresh memories of the incidents in the B.C. pen. Two residents of my constituency were held hostage during the last incident. Fourteen months ago, in a previous hostage taking, several of my constituents were involved in that one too, so I think I have a right to speak on that particular problem. 1 do not envy the job of the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) in trying to negotiate with criminals in that kind of situation. But there is something wrong when there are at least eight hostage takings within the one federal penitentiary within an 18-month period. Surely those prisoners have found that there is some kind of a reward bigger than the risk involved in that kind of activity. The balance is all screwed up.
We have a member of the citizens' advisory committee coming into the penitentiary and telling the RCMP how they ought to treat the prisoners. We have the prisoners being served hot meals while the guards on duty have cold lunches. Something is really all screwed up. We have local officials who

are deemed by Ottawa not to be smart enough to make decisions in a local emergency and therefore these officials have to funnel all suggested decisions back to Ottawa, with a delay of three or four hours before they can make a decision on the scene. We have a situation in which the federal government leases the most expensive floor space in Vancouver in the Pacific Centre but cannot find the money in order to provide more guards or stop overtime, or to provide the kind of training those guards need. The government says it must exercise austerity. This is the time it picks in which to exercise its austerity. I should like to refer to another aspect of this.
Another constituent of mine, named Marshall Green, was in a predicament a few months ago. He tried to prevent a murder. He states:
I managed to push the muzzle of the gun downwards before it went off, shattering my left leg at the groin. I then wrestled for possession of the gun with the man who appeared intent of finishing me off. Just as I passed out, witnesses arrived on the scene and disarmed my attacker, Kenneth Earl Marquardte.
The local RCMP charged Marquardte with attempted murder. He entered no plea when charged, was remanded for psychiatric assessment and was subsequently released on his own recognizance and $5,000 bail. The preliminary hearing was originally set for August 5 and I learned, only after I caused a number of telephone calls to be made in early August, that the hearing had been adjourned.
I heard nothing further from the Nakusp RCMP or the Crown prosecutor's office in Nelson. On Monday, September 13th, I received a newspaper clipping from the Nelson Daily News which stated that "Kenneth Earl Marquardte, 47, of Nakusp, was sentenced to five weeks in jail to be served on weekends and probation for six months on a charge of wounding with intent..

When I caused an inquiry to be made of the Crown prosecutor handling the case he confirmed that Mr. Marquardte had pleaded guilty to the charge of "wounding with intent" and that after his counsel had called two character witnesses and read in the psychiatric report, Marquardte was sentenced on September 2nd, 1976, as reported in the newspaper.

My concern is that I have lost my livelihood, have and will suffer terrible pain, will have to undergo extensive surgery at least twice, may loose the use of my leg forever; and my assailant has scarely lost any time away from his job after admitting that he tried to kill me.
Where is our sense of justice? It is not enough to have law and order. What we need is a balance in our approach to justice in our system.

Then he goes on to say:
I must now spend years in civil litigation against my attacker or elect to claim from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board who can only award a maximum of $15,000. Is that justice?
Is it any wonder that law abiding citizens, peaceful people in our country, are discouraged? I think that the throne speech is woefully lacking in the attention it pays to the needs of the common, ordinary citizens who are entitled to a return to
October 14, 1976

morality and justice, and to a balance in that area. Sooner or later we must come to a time when the criminal has to accept responsibility for the consequences of his behaviour. As I said before, a situation where prisoners get hot lunches and guards get cold lunches is not acceptable.
A fourth and final area to which I should like to address myself is in regard to the lack in the throne speech of any mention of the need for increased medical research. 1 know there will be others in my party who will address themselves to this matter, but again this is an ominous and condemning example of the scale of values that the government has established for itself: help to criminals, nothing for those who are incapable of helping themselves.
The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport dwelt on the need for social services, and I agree with this because we do need that kind of help. But she said nothing about the fact that the government has made cutbacks in medical research. I want to refer to some statistics, which admittedly are a number of years old, but that makes it even worse because since that time the government has cut back even more.
I wonder if hon. members are aware of the fact that Canada spends per capita only one sixth of the amount on medical research that the United States does. Canada spends $2.08 per capita and the United States spends $12.91. These statistics relate to the time before the government announced its so called austerity program and before it made cutbacks in funding for medical research several months ago. How much more shameful is the situation today.
I should like to refer hon. members to the statement made a few days ago by the president of the Association for the Mentally Retarded. Here we come to what could be construed as being very crass and cold dollar and cent statistics on the care of the mentally retarded. The president of that association said:
As an illustration, the lifetime cost of serving one person severely mentally crippled by a preventable condition or cause may be conservatively estimated at $400,000. For instance-
He gives the name of the disease which I cannot even sneeze out, let alone pronounce.
-phenylketonuria, a condition which produces massive brain damage, is one condition for which research has given us the means of detection and prevention. In a year, screening turns up an average of 20 PKU babies who, untreated, represent a potential lifetime bill to Canada of $8 million for each year's crop.
If you want to look at the crass dollar and cent expenditures you see you find what a foolish way it is to exercise austerity to take away money for medical research which would prevent this kind of expense. But how much more debilitating and soul destroying is the knowledge of all these people who are trying to help those who cannot help themselves, how much more discouraging is it for them to realize that here we have a government which is cutting back on medical research rather than trying to help those people who need help the most. This is the kind of government we have. It is time we had a restoration and a balance, as well as a sense of proportion, in the way in which the government applies its energies to help
The Address-Mr. O'Connell
those who cannot help themselves and make us a kind of people who can face each other with a sense of honour and dignity.
1 cannot in all conscience support the motion of the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and his colleague, as good as their speeches were, and I am happy to support the motion of our leader that we have no confidence in this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a subject with my colleagues in the House which deals with the matter of what we as a parliament can do to control government spending.
In the Speech from the Throne a subject matter was raised which I think is worthy of a rather prolonged debate in the House, that is, a debate between the proponents of a greater involvement of the state in the economy and the opponents of a deeper involvement of the state in the economy. However that debate may proceed, there is no doubt at all that there has been an enormous increase in the spending of the state and that this parliament, through its various committees, is not in a position, in my view, to control this government spending in the way that is expected of it. So the purpose matter of my remarks in the throne speech debate is to raise this issue among us and to make some suggestions of ways in which the government itself might contribute, and ways in which parliament by changing its committee structure might come to a better control of government spending. The stakes are very high, and they are not only in monetary terms.
The size of the public sector today is very large. It is estimated that governments at all three levels spend some 40 per cent or 39 per cent of the incomes in our country. They spend that proportion of the total economic effort registered as the Gross National Product. It may indeed be the view of some, which 1 do not share, that the public sector may become so large, or is already so large, that it may tend to destroy the very market system it is designed to support and regulate. We noted in the Speech from the Throne that the decision of the government was to proceed down a middle road as between increasing involvement or lesser involvement in the economy. Whether the government is able to proceed down this middle road will depend in some part on how this parliament can control government spending.
The point I am going to make is that we do not now control government spending except in a technical, legal or constitutional sense because, after all, parliament is the sovereign. But as a parliament we do not have the means-and I include hon. members on all sides of this House-to hold any government to the middle road, or to any other road, because we do not have the structures here which would enable us to play that role.
In my view it is urgent that we find new means of controlling government spending so that we can influence the degree of involvement which we feel appropriate for the state in the

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. O'Connell
market economy which we wish to see continued. It is urgent also because there is already such a built-in bias in public expenditure growth that, unless we find better mechanisms, the state will perforce play a much greater role, whether or not it is described as a middle road.
The suggestion I want to make is that the government itself should be publishing annually a white paper giving a five year record of what it has spent, in some detail, and including a five year forecast of what it plans to spend in the coming five years. For example, with the appropriate committee structure we should be able to look in some detail at what happened between 1971 and 1975 and with some considerable detail at what the government plans for the years 1976 to 1980 with respect to expenditures on all programs.
I think that such an annual white paper would put us in a position to grasp the totality of the increase in government spending spread over a period of time, and that it would show the extraordinary rise which has taken place. It would also no doubt show us that there is no real strategy for containment or reduction in the plans for the future. We would at least be in a better position, if we saw those plans, to exercise some judgment and restraint. We cannot exercise that judgment or control if we as a parliament do not have the mechanisms to do so. The case I am putting is that we do not have those mechanisms. I am going to ask also whether we have the will to create them. It is important to do so not just in terms of partisan debate over whether a program should be expanded or not, but, more significantly, whether the market economy will survive the incessant growth of the public sector, a growth which proceeds at rates of increase substantially in excess of the average growth rate of the economy. Therefore unless we find better mechanisms, the public sector will inevitably get larger and larger.
The white paper which I am suggesting on the part of the government-and in a moment I will come to parliament's part as opposed to the government's part-would also put hon. members in a position to tackle in a more effective way the question of wastage in expenditures.
And now what about ourselves as a group of members of parliament as opposed to ministers? I think we ought to admit that the experiment in having standing committees review the estimates is only a limited success. I personally doubt that the standing committee approach is adequate to our needs. I doubt it in part because we fragment our view of government spending when we deal with it by separate departments. For example, there is a group of 20 of us who will be considering the expenditures of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and another 20 who will be considering the expenditures of the Department of National Health and Welfare. And so it goes. But we do not have any vehicle by which we can look at the totality and the plans, and get an over view, and thus try to find some means of control, which is something more than a recording of what has been happening and a reporting back in a manner that is not really an effective control.
I think we must go beyond the standing committee approach to another device, and the suggestion I make is that we no

longer look at the estimates through the various 20 or so standing committees, but that we consider a single expenditure surveillance committee. Perhaps it should be quite large-40 members or so-because its members may have to divide into subcommittees. It seems we should have a single expenditures control committee or surveillance of expenditures committee- or call it what we will-which would examine, as the present standing committees do on a selective basis, some departments where there is special interest, grouped perhaps more into larger categories than presently. However, apart from looking at the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to use the same two examples, it would have as its main function the question of examining the over-all rates of spending, the over-all balances between departments and programs in terms of that five year plan which I have suggested, and in terms of what we on our part feel is appropriate for the dimensions of the public sector within the total economy and in terms of the requirements of a market economy for some control on this really unrestricted growth of the public sector.
The main duty would be to make comparisons, reach a view, and make greater efforts to get at the question of control, which parliament has really lost.
I think one of the questions which is most exercising our constituents today is control of government expenditure, and I do not think we are in a position to respond to them. That puts us in the position where we are going to face increasing cynicism about parliament as an institution. There is no doubt that the public is right, and it is not just because of the restraint program which is currently in operation. It is not just because expenditures have increased. It really is because of the basic issue of what is the role of the state in a market economy. We are not in an adequate position to influence that expect in ineffective debate. We need a mechanism which will help us contribute in terms of control of actual spending.
There is one other point I should like to make with respect to my suggestion for a new committee. It has been discussed recently in the House of Commons Committee on Procedure and Organization, as some hon. members will be aware. This kind of committee would be a counterpart, as it were, to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which looks at the record after the money has been spent; what we really need now is a similar over-view committee that looks at all the estimates taken together before they have been accepted. The present fragmented approach through the standing committees will not give us sufficient leverage to exercise the parliamentary function of control over spending before they are agreed to in the House.
A further point which is worthy of consideration is whether we ought to have the budget debate much closer in time- perhaps it cannot occur simultaneously with the estimates, but we should be looking at taxation and supply questions as well as spending questions much closer together in time.
October 14, 1976

I entered this debate on rather short notice, Mr. Speaker. While I feel this is one of the most important questions to which we could turn our minds, 1 also know that we will have an opportunity soon to look at the recommendations coming from the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization.
I hope we will give more attention to the matter of a revised committee system, certainly not from the point of view of change for the sake of change but to ensure that we can do our part to keep government on that middle road.

Mr. Speaker, along with my colleagues in this Chamber I am very pleased to participate in the opening debate of this second session of the Thirtieth Parliament. As a member who came here first in 1974, and having participated in the first session of this parliament which was the longest in the history of our country, I found it rather refreshing to hear the Speech from the Throne on Tuesday of this week. In many ways, even though 1 am in opposition, I was rather pleased with what I heard.
I think one should bear in mind though that a Speech from the Throne is nothing more than a collection of high-sounding words until the government decides to act or implement it. We should also remember that a good many of the promises made in the last Speech from the Throne have not been kept so perhaps I should review a list of those unkept promises.
In the last Speech from the Throne we were promised new consumer credit legislation, including the disclosure by lenders of effective rates of interest on loans; total revision of bankruptcy law to help the consumer debtor; the improvement of urban and inter-city transportation services; legislation to provide for an efficient port system; measures for government intervention in cases where a Canadian company may be prevented by its foreign ownership from fulfilling export orders; revisions to the Public Service Staff Relations Act; human rights legislation; provisions to broadcast the proceedings of the Commons. We see several of these items again in this Speech from the Throne. The government also has not delivered on guarantees for the domestic control of uranium mining. It makes me wonder just how much of this Speech from the Throne will be implemented.
I should like to quote some portions which I find encouraging, and yet which are hard to believe. The speech is reported in Hansard for Tuesday, October 12, and on page 2 there appears the following passage:
... the government will continue to practise fiscal restraint. The control of inflation will remain the single most important condition for economic stability in Canada, even after price and income controls are removed. Determined restraint in fiscal and monetary policy is essential to the long-term control of inflation.
I am puzzled when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) makes the statement that he is going to restrain government spending, and yet when we examine the facts we see that he is not. That is amazing, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister said exactly the opposite in his musings last New Year to what is
The Address-Mr. Elzinga
stated in the throne speech. At that time he said we needed more government intervention in the private sector.
In the New Year's Eve message the Prime Minister stated we were going to have more intervention in the private sector, yet in the Speech from the Throne he states that he would like to leave things more to the private sector. We have seen this flip-flop so often with this Liberal administration, Mr. Speaker. We saw it in 1972 when our party campaigned on certain proposals and was severely criticized for them, yet when this government was in a minority situation it implemented pretty well what we had campaigned on. In 1974 we saw exactly the same thing. As I said earlier, Mr..Speaker, I am still optimistic that it will implement certain areas of the Speech from the Throne and I feel that many are noteworthy.
Another promise which appears on page 2 of Hansard is as follows:
The government will introduce measures to assist small businesses by improving local access to financial assistance and other services provided by government departments, the Federal Business Development Bank, and financial institutions in the private sector.
The merger of the Unemployment Insurance Commission with the Department of Manpower and Immigration is also proposed. This is a measure which my good friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has advocated many times in this House. Moves are proposed in the area of labour-management relations. I think this is important and I hope some proposals are forthcoming. One only meeds to look around at the difficulties experienced on the labour- management scene today, such as the day of protest organized by the Canadian Labour Congress. Also mentioned is the National Transportation Act. We have been promised amendments to this act before, but to date no concrete steps have been taken to improve it.
One thing that is noteworthy is the absence of specific programs in an area that perhaps concerns the Canadian population more than any other, and that is the matter of criminal law or correctional philosophy.
There was no mention whatsoever of the constitution in the Speech from the Throne. We have seen how significant the constitutional debate is to the governing party with the resignation of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson).
As I have said on several occasions, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of politics is not to justify our own existence but rather it is to dedicate ourselves to the welfare of our country and its population. As my leader and others participating in this debate said so well, it appears that the government is concerned strictly with the winning of elections. There is a limit to the power of governments; they cannot solve all our problems. Therefore we must, as individuals concerned about the welfare of our country, strive to make this a better country for all our citizens, but I seriously question whether this government is doing that.
