speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the speech that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made earlier today, he made one statement which I thought was very important. As I took it down, these were his words: "This government has no intention of participating in or permitting a dismantling of the socially progressive society Canadians have built in this country." I regard that as a noble sentiment. It is one to which I hope we can hold this government.
It is true that during the last half century Canadians have managed to build a socially progressive society. At least we have moved in that direction. Most of it has come about since the end of World War I. Indeed, the greater part of it has come about since the experience this country had in the 1930's.
I may also say, as everyone knows, that most of it has been in the form of legislation we have won because of the prodding of those who have sat in this House under the leadership of the late J. S. Woodsworth, the late M. J. Coldwell, the present member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), David Lewis, and our present leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). It is true that governments of other parties have put the social legislation on the statute books, but what a struggle it has been to pry it out of them. However, now that we have it I am glad that this government states categorically that it does not want to participate in the dismantling of our socially progressive society.
None of us imagines that the government would actually dismantle that society by taking it apart or by abolishing some of the social legislation that has been passed. However, the main point I want to make in my remarks tonight is that the progress we have gained can be lost if it is not kept up to date. If the social legislation that is on our books is treated with indifference, treated as though we have achieved the last word and have nothing more to do, the value of that legislation can be whittled away just as much as if it were actually dismantled.
My plea tonight is that this government not forget its responsibility to make improvements in the pieces of social legislation that we have on the statute books of Canada.
I have quite a number of things that I want to mention, so I will have to speak briefly about each of them. I suppose in

effect what I am doing is indicating the things that I think ought to have been in the Speech from the Throne. If these things had been in the Speech from the Throne, it would have been a much brighter, more hopeful document than the one that was read to us a couple of days ago.
First, despite the fact that the Old Age Security pension is ever so much more in dollars today than it was when it was started back in the middle 1920's, most of our senior citizens 65 years of age and over are having a difficult time to get by. Even with the supplements they get in one form or another, in a society in which the cost of living is rising, and in which the standard of living is improving, thus creating a different milieu in which these people are living, they are finding it difficult to get by on the amount they receive.
In my view there ought to have been in the Speech from the Throne a commitment to increase the basic amount that is paid under the Old Age Security Act. That basic amount at the present time is $100 as specified in the act, plus the escalation that has taken place, which brings it during the present quarter to $139.39 a month. In my view that amount ought to be greatly increased. As a matter of fact, in light of today's cost of living and in light of our responsibility to our older people, it ought to be as high as $250 or $300 a month. But I suppose it is just as unrealistic to expect that substantial an increase all at once as it was when I argued that it ought to be $50 when it was only $30. However, we should be moving in that direction. What we should have before parliament at the present time is a proposal for a substantial increase in the amount of that pension.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I insist that the time has come for a lowering of the eligible age, certainly for all those who are out of the labour market. The spouses' pension that was introduced in June of last year recognizes that there are people between 60 and 65 who should be given a pension under the Old Age Security Act, but that is all that can be said for it. The means test on that spouses' allowance, and the fact that it is payable only to a person between 60 and 65 years of age married to and living with an older spouse, cut out widows, spinsters, widowers, bachelors-a great many thousands of people in that age bracket who are just as much in need of pension income as those who happen to meet the conditions of that provision. This, of course, would be taken care of if my proposal were accepted, namely, that all persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market should be entitled to receive the basic old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement as well. So I put that down as an item that is missing from the Speech from the Throne but which ought to be there.
While I am talking about old age pensions-and the same point applies to the rest of the pensions-I suggest the time has also come for a revision of the formula under which escalation takes place. Members on the government side frequently get up, as did the Minister of State responsible for fitness and amateur sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) this afternoon,
October 14, 1976

and tell us that the government has provided escalation that enables pensioners to keep up with the rising cost of living. It does no such thing; they are always behind. The consumer price index measures price increases in a general way and does not necessarily cover the things our elderly people actually have to buy. Whether it is quarterly or annual, it is always three or four months, eight or ten months, or even a year or more behind.
1 contend that the escalation formula should be put on a current basis so that in any quarter recipients of old age security or other pensions receive an escalation that will enable them to meet the rising cost of commodities in that very quarter. That is at the top of my list in the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker. These substantial improvements in the Old Age Security Act ought to be in that speech.
I call also for significant improvements in the Canada Pension Plan. There were doubts about this plan in some quarters when it was brought in, but it has proven to be a very successful piece of social legislation, so successful in fact that some of us think it should be greatly improved. The main improvement that in my view should be made is that the plan should be amended so that the pension that one receives on retirement is more than the present 25 per cent of one's average earnings over the prescribed period. There are those who have advocated that it should be as high as 75 per cent, but certainly we should move to 40 per cent or 50 per cent very soon.
There are two or three other aspects that ought to be improved. The requirement that a contributor be in the plan for three years before there is a survivor's benefit, or for five years before there is a disability benefit, does not correspond to ordinary insurance practices, and 1 think those provisions should be changed.
Tonight I wish to emphasize in particular that the two changes that the Minister of State referred to this afternoon, although they go in the right direction, do not begin to provide equality for women under the provisions of the Canada Pension Plan. Let me examine the two things that are being done, as outlined quite correctly this afternoon by the minister. First, there will be a provision that when marital breakdown takes place, whether divorce or separation, the total assets, whether there is one contributor or two, will be divided between the two partners fifty-fifty. But there is no improvement in the total situation of the two spouses; it is a case of splitting assets, and you only get a so-called advantage if you have a marriage breakdown.
The other provision that was announced this afternoon-at least, spelled out this afternoon; it has already been announced-is one regarding women who are in the work force and therefore contributors to the Canada Pension Plan, who take a few years off to stay in the home to raise their children, and who then subsequently go back into the work force. They will be permitted to drop out from the computation of their pension benefit those years that they spent at home.
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
That is fine, Sir, but what about the wives who have spent the whole of their married lives at home raising the children, looking after their children and their husband, playing their part in the life and work of that couple or family? There is nothing for them at all. They are not contributors so therefore do not get an advantage. The fine principles which were referred to by the Minister of State will not be realized until there is full equality. I realize she referred to the fact that there is equality at death: when a female contributor dies, she can leave the same benefit to her surviving widower that a male contributor can leave to his surviving widow.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is equality.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is equality that you get at death. You also get equality in terms of a fifty-fifty split in your marriage breaks down, and you get some consideration if you have been in the labour force, stayed out for a while to raise children, and then you return. But if you are an ordinary spouse at home the whole of your married life there is not one cent of benefit for you.
I contend that that is falling far short of equality between men and women. I noticed the other day that the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) asked the minister whether the references in the throne speech to pension improvements meant that housewives were now in the Canada Pension Plan. The very guarded answer that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) gave made it clear that they are not.
I know a little about the Canada Pension Plan. It is a wage related scheme, and there are technical difficulties working it out and so on. But we will not have done the fair thing and established the kind of equality that we talk about until there is for homemaker spouses, in one way or another, the same pension benefits that there are for women, spouses or single, who are out in the labour market. This is extremely important, and I hope in this session when we deal with human rights legislation and have more amd more said about equality between men and women that this will be done. It should have been included in the throne speech itself.
I am also sorry that there is no reference to the position of the blind and disabled. It used to be that every time we made improvements for other categories, their position was improved as well. But since we have got into old age security, the Canada Assistance Plan, into services and so on, there does not seem to be special consideration for the blind and disabled. 1 appreciate the fact that there is to be a social services act before us in this session and it may be that under it, with the co-operation of the provinces, something more will be done for all persons who need assistance. However, I am sorry we have reached the point where the blind and disabled do not get the special attention that I think they deserve.
I move on to list two or three more things that I feel should have been in the Speech from the Throne. One of them has to do with the position of retired civil servants, and I couple with them retired Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel and retired Canadian Armed Forces personnel. Generally speak-

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
ing, the pension plans respecting these groups have been greatly improved, but there are two or three pieces of unfinished business that some of us thought we were going to get resolved during the last session, especially when we were dealing with these matters before the special joint committee on employer-employee relations in the public service. However, in the end we lost out. It is most unfair that some persons who worked for the government in one way or another can get the escalation in their pensions prior to age 60 while others cannot. Those who feel this discrimination the most are retired RCMP personnel and retired members of the Canadian Armed Forces. That is a point I hope will be looked at more seriously during this session than was the case during the one that finished a couple of days ago.
I also press the point which again we thought we were going to have dealt with during the last session, and that is the position of the widows of any members of these groups, retired public servants, retired RCMP personnel or retired armed forces personnel, where the marriage took place after the contributor had gone on pension. In these days it can happen that the second marriage may last longer than the first one, yet we have this rule that denies to a widow in such cases the right to a pension when the husband dies. We had representations from delegations here during the last session who made the point extremely well and we were given the impression that the government was sympathetic, but in the end nothing was done to right this wrong.
Those are points that ought to be taken care of and there are others that affect retired public servants, retired RCMP and Canadian Armed Forces personnel, but I put these two points before the House with particular emphasis. I suggest there ought to have been references to them in the Speech from the Throne and I hope something will be done about them during the course of this session.
As I speak about these groups of retired persons I mention in particular the matter of escalation. Let me say that one of the most significant reforms we have won around here in recent years was the provision for the escalation in pensions at least in keeping with the rise in the cost of living. When we applied it to old age security we had to go on and apply it to retired public servants and all other groups, including those who draw war veterans' pensions and allowances. I deplore the kind of attack that occurs in some of the financial papers in this country against this principle of escalation. Usually the line is that others do not get it, so why should these groups get it? The answer to that is that all groups should get it. What we have started by way of providing escalation to old age pensions, pensions of retired public servants and others who work for the government, should be extended to apply to all pensions in both the public and private sectors.
Another area in respect of pensions which has concerned me all the years I have been in this place and which I think should have been in the Speech from the Throne has to do with pensions of retired railway workers, it is now over two years

since Dr. Noel Hall was commissioned to study and report on all railway pensions in Canada. I suppose the number of questions I have asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) about that report, such as when were we going to get it, is legion. I understand he does now have the report, that it is being translated, and that sometime fairly soon it will be tabled. I understand also it will be printed in large enough quantities so that all those who are interested will be able to get copies of this important report. The next step will be to implement the recommendations I am sure that report will contain.
I cannot imagine that Dr. Noel Hall could have spent two years examining the pension situation so far as railway workers in this country are concerned without coming up with recommendations that call for improvements. Many railway pensioners have died in the two years he spent carrying out the study. Let us not take two, five or ten years to make the improvements he will probably be recommending. We call for action soon, not just by the publicly owned Canadian National but by the privately owned Canadian Pacific as well.
As I say, that is another of the items 1 think should have been in the Speech from the Throne. I have already made the point that if the things I have been lining up for a throne speech had been there it would have been a much better document than the one read to us in the other place a couple of days ago.
I come to the last of the items I wish to mention and these have to do with veterans. First I should like to commend the Royal Canadian Legion on "Operation Service", a program or project the Legion has in effect right now under which it is trying to locate veterans, or their widows or survivors, who may not have known the benefits that were available to them, in the hope that they can now apply for and obtain those benefits. I am glad to see the publicity that has been given to this project, not only by the Legion itself but by others. I hope it will result in many cases of veterans or their survivors obtaining the benefits which are available to them but about which they have not known.
I am happy to say there have been improvements. The present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) has given us good leadership in this area and has fought hard for veterans in the Cabinet and we like what he has done. The fact is that this far away from the wars, and in a time of restraint, to get anything done for veterans is significant. We are glad that improvements have been made. But even in the last session when we were making the improvements involved in the bill that dealt with pensions for prisoners of war the government overlooked two or three things we had recommended, and I should like to put them in my proposals for a more adequate Speech from the Throne.
First of all, when we provided pensions for those who were prisoners of war we provided them only for those who were prisoners during World War II. We covered those in Hong Kong and in Europe, but there are still around aged veterans who served in World War I, who were prisoners of war and had horrifying experiences, yet they are not covered. The
October 14, 1976

number of dollars it would cost to provide pensions for the few of them around would be almost nothing. To have overlooked them I think was a disgrace, and I hope we may yet cover that inadequacy.
The government also erred, the committee did not, last session in not including pensions for those who were escapers or evaders. The prisoner of war compensation goes only to those who were actually in the prison camps, but there are others, at least one of whom is a member of this House, who spent months in Europe afraid for their lives as escapers or evaders, and it seems to me they should not be overlooked. I should like to see them included.
A very important recommendation was contained in the report of Dr. Hermann, and that had to do with widows of veterans on disability pensions. It was the same recommendation that Mr. Justice Mervyn Woods made when he gave us the Woods report several years ago.
As matters stand, if a war veteran is on a disability pension of 48 per cent or more and dies, his widow gets the full widow's pension, but if the veteran's disability pension is less than 48 per cent she gets zero-no pension at all. Mr. Justice Woods recommended, as did Dr. Hermann, that there should at least be pro rated pensions for such widows. Two or three times in the parliament before last, in the last one and in this one, the standing committee has recommended that this change be made, but the government turned us down. This ought to have been included in this Speech from the Throne. I hope it will be considered during the course of this session.
The other point I wish to make is that in terms of veterans' affairs some very real improvements should now be made in the War Veterans Allowance Act. It has been a good piece of legislation and has filled the bill in many cases where the Pension Act which provides war disability pensions did not, but it seems to me that this long after the wars we have had, at this stage when our veterans from those wars are getting into the upper years so far as age is concerned, we should move more in the direction of a guaranteed annual income for those veterans. I want a guaranteed annual income across the board. I hope we move in that direction and I hope the discussions between the federal government and the provinces produce something along that line soon-soon, please. But if it is going to take time to do this for the whole population at least we can start with an adequate and guaranteed annual income for war veterans, and this could be done under the aegis of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Minister of Finance in what he said this afternoon, that there should be no dismantling of the socially progressive society Canadians have built in this country. But that means more than just not taking destructive steps. It also means we must keep all these measures up to date. Therefore, I contend that the things that I have talked about tonight, such as improving old age security, the Canada Pension Plan, pensions for retired civil servants, pensions for RCMP and Canadian Armed Forces personnel, for retired railway workers and certainly for veterans and their survivors, are things which ought to have been in this year's Speech from
The Address-Mr. Lee
the Throne. If they had been it would be a much better speech than the one that is before us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always indeed a pleasure and honour to follow the last hon. member who just spoke very ably on the Speech from the Throne. As a member who had the honour and distinction of seconding the motion in reply to the Speech from the Throne in the first session of this parliament I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Resti-gouche (Mr. Harquail), and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), for their excellent speeches the other day. I should also like to congratulate all the new ministers on their appointments, particularly the new Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). He is certainly handling a difficult situation in the British Columbia Penitentiary very ably, and 1 look forward to working with him as his parliamentary secretary.
I rise to enter this debate to express to the people of my great riding of Vancouver East and my province how I feel the Speech from the Throne will better their lives. I do so not only as a British Columbian but as a westerner. What is a westerner?
In my speech during the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne in October, 1974, I attempted to define a westerner as follows:
It is true that Canada is made up of many diversified regions and economies. It is equally true that western Canada in its make-up is not homogeneous but is, in reality, very heterogeneous. There are, however, some regional traits common to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
First, industries in western Canada are predominately resource-oriented. Second, westerners are individualists; each of us has a feeling that we can make our own way and direct our own life. Third, westerners judge a person for what he or she is, and not so much on the basis of where he or she comes from. Fourth, westerners take great pride in our earnest hopes for a unified Canada based on the diversity of our ethnic origins.

No; it is from my speech during the last session. Because of these regional traits we feel that the west is unique. We are more confident. We are more optimistic. We are more outward looking. Economically most of us westerners believe in the free enterprise system and undoubtedly welcome decentralization of decision-making, especially decision-making on the federal scene. That is why I, as a westerner, am gratified to see this government outlining a legislative program that strengthens the faith in the individual and strengthens the capacity of the market system. Among other things, the encouragement to small business, and the Human Rights Act are welcome words to westerners.
What does the west want?

We want to do our own thing. We want to shape our destiny in Confederation. One thing which we westerners want is an atmosphere in which individual enterprise and the

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Lee
market economy can thrive. I shall not reiterate the reasons and the encouraging results of the government's control program, for others have done so. I would, however, like to say a word about the day of protest.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Lang and Goodale have got to go.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
An extreme amount. He is a westerner as well.
The labour movement has held a day of protest against the anti-inflation program. The methods used by some of the trade union leadership in seeking the support of their rank and file membership have unquestionably cast a shadow upon their credibility and, more important, have left many of their rank and file with doubt that their leadership believes in the protection of one of the hallmarks of our great democracy, namely, the freedom to dissent.
A peaceful protest is a part of a democratic tradition, and I support the right of any and all Canadians to make representations to the government or to criticize governmental policy at any time. But from my point of view the trade union leadership has not made the right decision on the anti-inflation program. The program to restrain prices and wages was the government's response to a world inflationary trend which, in Canada's case, was combined with an unacceptably high level of employment. For some weeks before the program was introduced public opinion polls showed that the majority of Canadians wanted the government to do something to stop inflation and turn it back.
This time last year an inflation rate of more than 10 per cent a year was making it very difficult, if not impossible, for ordinary Canadians to make ends meet. Fear of still higher prices was causing trade unions to ask for wage increases of 20 to 25 per cent or more in a one-year contract. Companies were unable to predict their costs even three months ahead and they were forced to make their prices subject to revision without notice.
Nobody likes controls. I don't like them. The government does not like them. We would all like to get out of controls as soon as possible. Critics of the program are insisting that the government get out of the program now. But this is not what the majority of Canadians want. The polls show Canadians have some reservations about some aspects of the program, but they want the restraints to continue, at least for a temporary period.
Since the program came into effect we have made some encouraging improvements in price levels. Prices are still going up, but not as fast as a year ago, and remember it is a control program, not a freeze. In September the rate of increase in the consumer price index was 6.5 per cent over September 1975. This compares with a rate of 10.6 per cent a year ago.
On the wages and salary side, the Anti-Inflation Board is approving increases that average between 11 and 12 per cent for 1975-76. It is quite obvious that workers are now keeping ahead of inflation, whereas a year ago wages were falling behind price increases. On average, workers are 4 per cent

better off in real take-home dollars, not inflated dollars, than they were a year ago.
I hope that labour's day of protest did not involve any breaches of the law. We all recognize the right of citizens to protest against government policy, but a general strike could breach collective agreements and therefore could be illegal. The labour movement has a vested interest in maintaining its collective agreements.
Following the day of protest I urge trade union members to get behind the program and help us reach to our goal sooner. I also urge them to tell their leadership to accept the invitation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to continue the consultation meetings which were started last June. The door is still open.
Another thing we westerners want is a unified Canada based on the diversity of our ethnic origins. We westerners regret the resignation of the former minister of national defence, one of our spokesmen in government. Although I respect his decision, I believe it was premature. The discussions and negotiations between the federal government and the provincial governments regarding the patriation of the constitution have not been concluded. Unfortunately I feel that his resignation has again crystallized the issue of billingualism.
As a Canadian of Chinese ancestry, who has unfortunately lost most of the use of the Chinese language, I can understand and sympathize with those who wish to preserve the French language in Canada. This worth-while and earnest attempt to preserve and foster the French language is not an easy goal to obtain. The government has recognized this in the Speech from the Throne by placing more emphasis on teaching French in the schools.
Certainly it is difficult being a western representative. Often when I travel in western Canada I hear words such as these, "You should be ashamed of yourself, selling out western Canada to Quebec-let them separate". I can assure my fellow westerners that it is equally difficult being a representative from Quebec. My colleagues from Quebec, I am sure, often hear words such as, "What are you doing there in Ottawa selling out our interests to English speaking Canada? Let us separate".
Canadians in the past have faced, and undoubtedly in the future will face, these emotional questions. As a westerner I am confident that we will respond positively because we westerners take great pride in our earnest hopes for a unified Canada based on the diversity of our ethnic origins.
I wish to touch on another thing that we westerners want. We westerners want freer trade. First, let me lay a myth to rest. Let us consider the Canadian tariff. Protectionism costs Canadians money-Canadians from coast to coast. Beat protectionism down and everyone will benefit, easterners and westerners alike. We are all consumers whether we live west of the Rockies or east of the Ottawa river. Do away with import duties and we will all be better off from an economic point of view.
October 14, 1976

What then is the present political climate for this long standing dream which we westerners have? Trade policy, or to use the term that economists prefer, commercial policy, is a matter of the highest importance. In fact it relates to a subject that is centuries old. But the fact remains that it is more important today than ever to determine whether we are to establish our policy by basing ourselves on the past or by looking toward the future. The problem was most recently brought up very forcefully in a report of the Economic Council of Canada in a document entitled "Looking Outward" which deserves very special attention.
Essentially the Economic Council of Canada's report suggests that Canada adopt a new commercial policy. This policy would be one that has always been advocated by westerners, namely, freer trade. The logic of those who drew up the report lead them to say freer trade would mean greater producer specialization, production spread over a longer period of time, and lower costs. As for the consumer, he or she would benefit from a movement toward freer trade in that prices would be reduced both for imported products and for products manufactured in Canada, while at the same time he would have the advantage of the wider choice of goods to purchase.
What is of equal, if not even of greater importance, is that the council maintains that unless we adopt a freer commercial policy, our relative position internationally will continue to deteriorate. Already it can be observed that during the past few years Canada has gone from our traditional second to eighth place in terms of our standard of living. Although I realize that such international comparisons of standards of living are subject to technical criticism, the fact remains that such a relative decline gives food for thought. I believe that Canada should adopt a gradual policy which works towards freer trade.
1 believe that the conclusions of the Economic Council of Canada on this subject are correct and therefore should have generated a much wider national debate than they have before. We must debate openly and candidly what our intentions should be as regards the future of our commercial and industrial policy. The issue is not a partisan one, it should not be a regional one, and it must be addressed soon. It must concern labour as well as management. Long after our price and income controls are finished and forgotten, the consequences of the policy decisions taken over the next few years will affect the lives and livelihood of Canadians well into the 1990's.
I am concerned that to date the report has generated so little discussion. I must say that whatever discussions have taken place have left me somewhat disappointed by their superficial and, let's say the word, frequently too nationalistic character.
I take the liberty of emphasizing the fact that we must not confuse our more emotional short-term feelings with a rational analysis of what could be beneficial for all the provinces of this country over a long period of time. The 23 recommendations made by the Economic Council of Canada illustrate clearly the exhaustive and practical nature of its analysis of Canadian commercial and industrial policy. Oriented toward the reduction or abolition of tariff and non-tariff barriers to internation-
The Address-Mr. Lee
al trade over a period of time, they do not neglect various matters connected with foreign investment and the operation of multinational companies. Moreover, the council looks at and recognizes the problems related to economic dislocation, the adjustment process, and the additional administrative requirements.
1 want to reiterate that my primary objective and hope as a westerner are to generate a much more vigorous and positive debate on the whole body of problems posed by the report of the council. That report must absolutely be given every consideration, and I encourage the government to do so.
Perhaps it would be a good idea at this point to summarize the basic advantages that greater freedom of international trade would have for Canada. Forecasts for economic gain from the elimination of tariffs are from 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the Gross National Product. As regards producers, Canadian corporations would benefit from the specialization which would be brought about by increased access to foreign sources of raw materials and to foreign markets.
This would enable them to use their capital more effectively by channelling it into activities where there was higher productivity, and by reducing under utilization. In the same way, workers could benefit from better paid jobs since their productivity would be higher. It is believed that Canada will have to face a probable shortage of workers during this decade. Consequently, according to the council, possible unemployment should not be a major obstacle to the enactment of its recommendations.
The advantages Canadian consumers could draw from a liberalization of trade are evident. The effect of the reduction or abolition of import duties on goods entering Canada would be to reduce or even eliminate some hidden subsidies presently paid by consumers. Even if this means only a few cents here and there, over-all import tariffs represent quite a heavy price to pay for the maintenance of often short term production opportunities in Canada. As a secondary consequence greater interdependence between nations through liberalization of trade should dampen domestic inflationary pressures, a result which must also be considered beneficial to consumers, particularly those people on fixed incomes.
The recommendations of the council are therefore aimed essentially at the liberalization of Canada's international trade with other countries on as broad a basis as possible. Thus the council feels we should do everything in our power to lower both our own barriers to trade and those of other countries by seeking to form free trade associations with other countries, for example, with the United States, the European Community, and Japan.
I repeat that I am here as an advocate of freer trade, but one who realizes the issues are complex and there are no easy solutions. I do feel, however, that the council's report is a serious effort to deal in a practical fashion with a body of economic problems which Canada will have to face in the coming years.

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Lee
Aside from the more or less traditional arguments that I have cited about basing international trade on the most productive industrial sectors of a country, the economic council also emphasizes the appearance on the scene of other international forces which indicate that trade liberalization offers a more advantageous future for Canada.
Among the trends that have developed during these last decades, one of the most significant is without doubt the creation of integrated international economic systems. While 20 years ago there were more than 20 developed countries in the non-Communist world, each having an essentially separate economy, today we are confronted with the economic superpowers, namely, the United States, the European Economic Community, and Japan. The other economic entities seem very small by comparison with this trio of giants. The thrust of expansion in these affluent economies is generally orientated toward industrial activities requiring advanced technology and intensive utilization of intellectual resources. In the manufacturing sector, at any rate, the key to efficiency is modern organization of production, that is, large-scale production necessitating a vast industrial infrastructure and a very high degree of product specialization.

speechtext: Is this still the west you are talking about, Art?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, it is something I hope your party stands for as well, freer trade.
The emergence of a certain number of new "Japans" is a phenomenon of equal importance. These are developing countries-Taiwan and Singapore, for example-which show great ability to produce technologically uncomplicated goods such as those Japan manufactured before the Second World War. And as was the case in Japan in that era, the wages paid by industries in those countries are relatively low, labour is industrious, their machinery is advanced technologically, and hence their products are quite inexpensive.
These countries export a large part of their production to the richer, more industrial countries such as Canada, where they easily compete with comparable, although more expensive, local products.
These changes in the international economy are of particular importance for a country such as Canada, for while we are an economically advanced state, the size of our internal market is too small to enable us to increase adequately our level of efficiency through mass production and specialization in our manufacturing sector. This situation limits our ability to compete with the production of the major industrial nations and the newly industrialized areas of the Third World. This is increasingly the case not only in foreign markets but also even within Canada. Moreover, it tends to prevent Canadian industries from undertaking the development of technological innovations which could make up for the disadvantages stemming from high unit costs.
Canada is thus caught in a vise between industrialized countries and developing countries. As time goes on this pressure on Canadian industry will continue to get more intense.
The practical character of the council's recommendations therefore is underlined by the emphasis placed on the need to establish an over-all major program of industrial readjustment with high employment, of which the costs would be a matter of community rather than individual responsibility. As hon. members can see, this is the only equitable course, insofar as Canadian society as a whole is concerned, which will reap the benefits of trade liberalization.
The practical nature of the council's recommendations is also reflected in recognition of the fact that it will be extremely difficult for Canada to gain increased access to foreign markets. Although since the Second World War there has been a notable drop in the customs duties charged by the industrialized countries, particularly from the prohibitive levels they had reached in the 1930's, there has been observable for some time an appreciable multiplication of the noncustoms barriers which have the impact of restraining foreign competition. Not only will these non-customs barriers be more difficult to remove, since it is easy to justify them for reasons such as, for example, national security or fraud protection requirements or dangers to health and safety, but the mere detection and defining of these barriers pose numerous problems which must be overcome if trade liberalization is to have any real meaning. In short, our country must be prepared to make concessions in some important areas of domestic policy in order to remove obstacles to our exports.
Nevertheless, the most relevant argument advanced by the Economic Council in support of its recommendations is precisely one which I mentioned earlier, namely-according to some statistics-the drop from second to eighth position internationally in Canadian income per capita, since the Second World War. If at least some of the changes advocated by the council are not made in the commercial and industrial policy of Canada, low productivity levels could remain a problem for our country, and its international position or the real income per inhabitant could continue to fall relatively in the 1980's and 1990's. The question is whether Canadians are prepared to accept this to protect the status quo.
If the answer is affirmative, then they need not heed the recommendations of the Economic Council. But if the answer is negative, then they will at least have to examine carefully and discuss the matters raised by the council.
In conclusion, I strongly feel, as a westerner, that there should be a much more vigorous debate on the Economic Council's report on commercial and industrial policy. If I have encouraged the government to read this report, which will not grow stale over time, and to think about it in the months to come, I shall have attained my goal. Thank you for your attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pride in rising to speak so early in the debate on the Speech from the Throne in this second session of the Thirtieth Parliament. It is also interesting to follow the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who spoke a few
[Mr. Lee.)
October 14, 1976

moments ago on the need for increased pensions. It almost makes one wonder whether he ought not to have been declared to have a conflict of interest for the stand he took.
I was amused, though, at the rather latex imagination displayed in the interpretation of the Speech from the Throne made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee). 1 could commend the hon. member, however, for some of the other thoughts he expressed. The only sad thing is that those thoughts were not expressed in the Speech from the Throne nor was there any indication that they might be used in forthcoming legislation.
A careful reading of the Speech from the Throne indicates that it must have taken a search of two volumes of the thesaurus to find a definition of the world "hollow"; I am sure this is the only Speech from the Throne that will echo when we drop it.
The Liberal party told Canadians in 1974 that the issue was leadership. 1 think there was nothing in this country's history as important as October 12 to demonstrate that that is a fact. That is probably the only true statement they made in the 1974 leadership campaign.
There was one omission from the speech that I think was obvious to every Canadian. If we recall for a moment the first session of the Thirtieth Parliament we remember that two of the important thrusts at that time were the abolition of capital punishment through Bill C-84, and the accompanying Bill C-83, the act to tighten up security in this country. Virtually every Canadian recognized that Bill-83 was simply a cosmetic measure to try to get the capital punishment bill through this House.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that our prisons have been getting very drafty lately; people are going in and out of prison just like they go in and out of the theatre. It was a natural follow-up to the last session that there be something in this Speech from the Throne about law and order. The problem has been documented by recent events, particularly in the federal prisons and most particularly the prison in New Westminster, British Columbia.
There is in Canada today what we would have to call a law and order crisis. If we were really to talk about security in this country under a Liberal government, we would conclude that we would have greater security if the citizens were locked up and the prisoners let go free.
Bill C-83 introduced in the last session of this parliament was in truth nothing more than a gimmick to get Bill C-84 through the House. That has been proven by the fact that in the Speech from the Throne there was no further thrust toward peace and security in this society. This flies in the face of some very devastating facts, and we note that the gun control legislation was really a fly coil collection of concepts jumbled together in a manner that in no way linked one to the other. It was put before the House, and dragged on for months on end simply because the government had not made a sincere or earnest attempt to do something about law and order.
The Address-Mr. Malone
I think it is time we looked at some of the facts relating to peace and security in this country to see exactly what is happening. In a recent 12-month period four prison employees have been killed; since 1970 60 prisoners have committed suicide, 14 inmates have been slain, and a much larger number were bludgeoned, beaten or stabbed. In the last ten years there has been a 90 per cent increase in violent crimes. Three out of every four prisoners are graduates of the prison system. Prisoners are simply being recycled. We do not have a prison system in Canada; all we do is reintroduce them to their old homes.
Last year we spent $256 million to house some 9,000 men and women in federal penitentiaries, which is three times the amount spent only seven years ago. If the annual prison bill continues to increase at this rate, by 1984 it will be in excess of $1 billion. I think we have to ask ourselves to what extent are we going to provide federal funds, government funds, taxpayers' funds for a prison system that is not working.
There is no doubt when you get well over three-quarters of the prisoners re-entering the prison system, when you get stabbings and killings taking place at the present rate, when the prisoners are becoming the rulers of the prisons, that there was an obvious need for something in the Speech from the Throne that dealt with law and order. That was omitted, and it simply underscores that Bill C-83 was gimmickry when it was introduced in the last session. The government talked about peace and security but it had only one thing in mind, and that was the abolition of capital punishment. It achieved this without giving Canadians an assurance that it would do something about peace and security. I think more Canadians would have accepted the abolition of capital punishment had the government acted in exactly the reverse way-had it done something about peace and security first and then come in with a position on the abolition of capital punishment.
The annual cost of maintaining a prisoner in a maximum security prison is 60 per cent more than the average Canadian industrial worker earns. I think that underscores one of the faulty priorities we are imposing upon our society-when we simply recycle people at a maintenance cost considerably higher than the average Canadian is earning today.
The basic cause of the problems in our prison system is the government's ambivalence and its confused policy on peace and security. The government is in a spin; it is totally unsure of its priorities. It does not know whether a prisoner should be rehabilitated, whether he should be punished, or whether the intent of prisons is to protect the public. On any one of those objectives ministers tinker and experiment at great risk to the public at large. I think we can say with considerable assurance that the government owes it to the Canadian people to come forward with something in a Speech from the Throne that will guarantee to Canadians a sense of security and a feeling of peace.
In this country we have the wrong attitude toward first offenders. Through the judicial system, first offenders today are getting off without any form of punishment whatsoever. In fact once a first offender is released it often happens that he is simply enticed, by the system itself, to repeat the crime.

October 14, 1976
The Address-Mr. Malone
Anyone who has ever trained a horse or a dog, anyone who has ever worked in the field of child psychology, is well aware that bad behaviourial patterns should not be allowed to be repeated time and time again. There can be no hope of successful rehabilitation that way.
Every farm boy knows that you cannot allow a dog access to the chicken coop all summer long and then in the fall of the year attempt to train him to keep out of it. Our court system today is saying that when a person commits an offence for the first time he should be allowed out on probation or let go free. What 1 am saying does not necessarily mean of course that every first offender should end up in jail; it just means that every first offender should be given some penalty.
If the government had any imagination it would design a system that would show first offenders that when you do not live within the law you have to face the consequences. I think that concept is missing from our law and order system today. Those who have disobeyed the law and have been the gainers because they disrespected the law obviously will be encouraged to repeat the commission of crimes. One of the most important omissions from the Speech from the Throne is this; the speech says nothing about law and order. That is to say, there is no hint at follow-up legislation to that proposed in the first session of the thirtieth parliament.
May I now deal with another subject of tremendous consequence to Canadians. I submit that misleading information coming from the federal government has caused tremendous damage to some regions of Canada and brought about what some in this country today call the beef crisis. People who talk about this crisis are really talking about the low prices cattlemen are getting for livestock to be sold for slaughter, that is, for beef.
in this country there is not a crisis in the beef marketing system; the crisis has to do with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). What has happened since the minister assumed his responsibilities? Between 1973 and 1974 we heard 29 ad hoc, short-term policy pronouncements affecting the beef industry, the third largest industry of this country. Those 29 ad hoc, short-term pronouncements tended to disrupt the market, alienated our American friends, and put ranchers and cow-calf producers in a net loss position, in that their production costs exceeded income. Sadly lacking is any long-term policy in this field. That is shameful. The meat packing industry is this country's largest food producing industry, and the third largest industry over-all.
Let us consider some data to see how important meat is in the economy. For example, please note that annually some 200,000 freight cars filled with meat products are shipped in this country. The meat industry is, as I said, this country's third largest; it is a $2.5 billion industry which pays $265 million in wages and salaries to employees here. Approximately 275,000 ranchers across Canada supply materials for the meat industry. Interestingly, about 80 per cent of Alberta cattle killed weekly ends up in the Montreal consumer market.
[Mr. Malone.)
I do not for a moment think that the importation of beef from Oceanian countries, that is, from New Zealand and Australia, an importation which has depressed the meat industry of this country, has come about by accident. It is my firm conviction that our federal government planned such importation in order to keep meat prices down because it wanted to show that its anti-inflation program is working. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in the Atlantic provinces he repeated, again and again, that the anti-inflation program is working. It was suggested that this is evident because food prices in recent months rose 6 per cent, whereas one year ago they were rising at the rate of 10 per cent. He repeated the same message in southern Ontario. As recently as one or two days he again said, on television, that the anti-inflation program is working because the cost of food is down.
The truth is that the cost of food is not down. One would find, if one itemized all food costs, that the price of all food except pork, poultry, and beef has risen. Consumers have made major savings in beef. In other words the Liberal government, which has most of its support and seats in two provinces of Canada, is saying to the ranchers and producers of Alberta and the other prairie provinces that they are expendable. The government is writing off the prairie provinces. It recognizes that it has no seats from Alberta. It is saying that it does not care about the damage it is doing to the enterprising ranchers of the prairie provinces: they are considered as expendable. Therefore the government intends to import cheap beef from Oceanian countries, beef which is sold at low prices, in order to prove that the anti-inflation program is working. That is an insensitive and callous position. It is wrong to fight inflation on the backs of those who are made the victims of a crisis brought about by the importation of cheap beef to this country. It is wrong in this way to write off certain voters.
Remember, we had a surplus of meat in this country because of the policies this government introduced in the first place. They date back to when the Liberal government introduced the LIFT program, which was designed to encourage farmers to take land out of grain production and seed it to grass. This policy encouraged the production of cattle. I submit that the LIFT program ought to have been called the goof program. That program brought about an increase in the country's cattle population, to the extent that as of February, one year ago, the cow and heifer population of this country had increased 45 per cent over that of one year before. We saw high levels of domestic over-production of beef, and now we see the devastating results of an increase of 139 per cent in beef imported from New Zealand, and of an increase of 10 per cent from Australia. This is wrong. The government is writing off people in regions where it has no political support. Is it any wonder that the government seems to be dividing the country instead of unifying it?
The government's policies are at fault. There is nothing wrong with Canada. I do not take the position that Canada is a country divided by nature. What is wrong is this: the government's policies have pitted one part of the country against another. Putting it another way, the government has
October 14, 1976

tried to trade off the loss of votes from the raw material and producing areas of this country against the gain of votes in the large transportation and population centres, which by their nature contain a larger number of seats and votes.
Let me repeat the importance of the meat industry to Canada. It makes annual sales of about $2.5 billion, is the third largest manufacturing industry of this country, ranks second from the standpoint of materials used, materials worth over $2 billion, spends about $5 million every day on livestock purchases, employs over 31,000 people, and pays $265 million annually in wages and salaries. Further, it contributes over $20 million annually in income taxes, and spends over $13 million annually for fuel and electricity. Yet the government is willing to write off that entire sector of the economy in the prairie provinces and southern British Columbia. It is saying these people are expendable, and it is doing this to prove that its anti-inflation program is working.

May I refer to something else, which, ironically, shows what is happening in this country. The Prime Minister has created a new portfolio and appointed a new minister in charge of small business. Who can deny the importance of such a portfolio? Obviously it is important for us to give more attention to small business in this country. But the fact is, as can be documented again and again with good examples, the services and policies of the government are deliberately driving away small business from this country. If there is anything that could underscore that better, it would be a review of what the postal system is doing in relation to small business.
We are getting absolutely terrible service from two major post offices in my home province, namely, Edmonton and Calgary. In one rural post office in my constituency complaints have been received from Medicine Hat, Armstrong, B.C., Salmon Arm, B.C., Kamloops, B.C., Oshawa, Ontario and Edmonton.
One constituent who receives a regular mailing of a weekly paper has kept a record of dates on which he has received it. He received a paper on June 21 that was mailed on June 2, one on June 21 that was mailed on June 9, one on June 30 that was mailed on June 23 and one on August 17 that was mailed July 28.
Letters to the publisher of a local weekly from a disgruntled client states that it takes ten days for the paper to get from
The Address-Mr. Malone
Stettler to Medicine Hat by mail, and eight days to Edmonton. The fact is that people can walk to either of those places in half that length of time. That is a literal fact. Virtually anyone, except the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), could walk from my constituency to Medicine Hat, but it takes ten days to get the mail delivered that distance.
One weekly paper laments that if the poor service continues, in due course it will be out of business. The government has the gall to give us what it calls a minister of small business while at the same time its actions and policies are driving small business out of a profit situation.
There are two or three other things I would like to put on record with regard to the Speech from the Throne. One deals with a request for an investigation into farm implement service. When the harvest season rolls around in the fall of the year, that is the time when grain people make almost all of their annual income. It might be said that a grain farmer can make several hundred dollars an hour during the harvest season. However, during this past harvest season the equipment repair situation was nothing less than atrocious. For example, on a major combine produced and serviced in the prairie provinces, there is a particular "V" belt. If that had broken on a machine this past summer, there was not another one available in any of the three western provinces.
It has also been reported and calculated that in numerous communities there have been waits of over two weeks for replacement parts for farm machinery during the harvest season. That should point out graphically that during the two to three weeks harvesting season, depending on good weather, parts for farm machinery should be available. There should be an investigation into the whole supply and service of the implement situation in this country.
It is incumbent upon the government to cause an investigation and have a hearing in the farm communities so that people involved in farming can voice their concerns and complaints. There should be some rectification of this problem that is causing serious economic concern in the wheat and grain producing areas of the prairie provinces.
It is not right for some people to be able to harvest a bumper crop when, because of a mechanical breakdown and having to wait several weeks for replacement parts, their neighbours must suffer a devastating loss.
I note also from the Speech from the Throne that the government intends to increase the status or importance of the female in society. While I commend and applaud those words, I cannot help but be suspect about their content.
We recently witnessed what was labelled International Women's Year. It was really nothing more than a $3 million campaign of "Why not?" buttons. That is no way to treat women in our society. If we did a study of what has happened to females in this country in terms of improvement of their status since International Women's Year, we would not see any improvement in the hiring rate of women in the public service. There has been no real improvement in terms of

legislative action in relation to women. The only thing that would be demonstrated, and demonstrated soon, in terms of women in this country that would help upgrade their status would be an increase in the number of women in the House of Commons.
I wish to give a concrete example. The government should take legislative action in relation to farm wives. Anyone associated with farming or ranching communities is well aware that the farm wife often works just as hard as the farmer. They work side by side. She often drives farm equipment and machinery, trucks grain in the fall of the year, and puts in a 15 to 16 hour a day during spring seeding and fall harvesting. What an insult it must be to that farm wife in April when her husband writes her off in income tax for $1,644. He could hire a man, but he cannot pay his wife. If he did, it would be considered as part of the family income. If the government is sincere about attempting to do something for females in this country, that is one place it could start to do something meaningful.

In a collection of throne speeches the government has talked about what it is going to do for women. It is high time that the women in this country asked when this action is going to come about. It should again be repeated that the best symbol of what will happen with regard to improvement in the status of women in this country will happen on October 18.
I wish to spend some time discussing another extremely neglected area in terms of the Speech from the Throne. I refer to the government's commitment to do something about the elderly in our society. Being elderly is not treated as a stage in the development of life. In many ways these people are treated as though they were a separate species. They are taken out of the main stream of society, often put into homes or, more often, made to feel as though they are without purpose, without participation, citizens of a different status from others in the adult society.
I cannot think of a more real plight or blight in society than the treatment given to senior citizens in this country. One answer might be to expend more money in terms of pensions. That might help to some degree. However, a government with any imagination would realize that the problems being faced by senior citizens go far beyond the simple financial status. They should be able to participate and have the opportunity to become fully involved in doing something. True, it may be at a slower rate; true, it may not be at the same pace. They are able to participate in their younger years, but there has not been a structural system set up in Canada today to allow these people in their golden years to have an opportunity to feel useful, as if they are people of self-esteem who can do something. This is robbing us of a great deal of talent, and moreover is creating tremendous expense not only in terms of human happiness but in terms of social cost and medical bills. It also treats them in a way in which we really would not want to treat the most
[Mr. Malone.)
lowly person in this country. The fact of the matter is that Canada was built by the senior citizens of this country.

I have not come to the commending yet but to what she might do. Whenever we talk of fitness and sport, the general emphasis is on the youth. I hope the new minister in charge of fitness and sport will take it within her jurisdiction to look at senior citizens' homes. Because in truth, while they may not be the kind of people who will be challenging for Olympic competitions of some kind, fitness obviously is important to our senior citizens, just as it is important to the health of any other age group in society.
If there is any place where we need to talk about fitness and the availability of physical exercising equipment, it must be in relationship to our senior citizens. When we stop and think of the very poor architectural design of our senior citizens' homes, the fact that residents are often cooped up in one room with a hallway down to the dining lounge and with a piano at the other end, when we recognize that fitness is important to the whole circulatory and respiratory system, one of the things we should do is to expand the concept of fitness and sport beyond our young people to the senior citizens of our country. If we are talking about the health of a group of senior citizens, people who can fully participate in and contribute to our society, then it is incumbent upon us to try to extend to them all the amenities of life that are traditionally enjoyed by anyone of adult age.
One other concept I should like to put forward for the consideration of the House is that it would do us well to give consideration to establishing in each province in Canada a co-op store in which senior citizens can sell their products, such as doilies, pillow cases, sheets, bookends-whatever it may be-and receive a significant tax break. I make that suggestion on this basis. The truth of the matter today is that we always talk of giving more money to our senior citizens.
October 14, 1976

What we fail to do is provide an avenue by which senior citizens might become participants in their own well-being.
Whether this example I have given is utilized or not, it is imperative that we discover a method whereby senior citizens are able to advance their own status economically, have a sense of participation and a feeling that somehow they have gained more self-esteem because they are able to take part in the social and educational structure of Canada. A senior citizen has to be treated like a regular human being, not as a species separate from the rest of society. In other words, we need a whole rethinking as to how we analyse and talk about our senior citizens.
In the same vein, when talking about how the throne speech fails to recognize senior citizens, we should also take a look at the age group that is soon to become a senior citizen. In truth it can be documented by a considerable number of psychologists and sociologists that the vast majority of Canadians, without a shadow of a doubt, are not prepared for their retirement years. What happens is that they go into psychological depression following their working careers, and this often happens because no program has been established in this country, either through the industrial factory or by the public service, to prepare people for a meaningful, creative and involved retirement.
In the provinces and through the dominion government we provide a health scheme that pays for medical costs. What we have failed so miserably to do is to establish a preventative medicine system. In the same way, there is no preventative system in the social justice sphere that we spoke of earlier when talking about the prison system. I think we need to readdress ourselves not only to the problem of inflation but to our prisons, to agriculture, an area in which this country is falling far short of its potential, to the problems of our senior citizens, and more important, to opportunities for every region to be able to feel like it is a part of Canada, linked together by some kind of transportation system.
The subject of transportation has been in the throne speech for I do not know how many times now, but I do know that for at least the sixth time the Department of Transport has promised a complete review of the rail network on the prairies. Such a review is now back in the throne speech and all we can hope is that this promise will culminate in some action that is over 100 years late in coming. This has left the prairies still the producer of raw material and has made central Canada the sole manufacturing area of this country. The three prairie provinces are placed in a tremendous deficit position in the economic sense because of an inequitable freight rate structure.
It does not make sense that we in this country have a freight rate system under which it is cheaper to ship products from Toronto to Vancouver than it is to ship products from Toronto to Calgary. Nor should it be in this country that we have a kind of freight rate structure in which rapcsced as a raw material per rolling ton costs half as much to ship in the same kind of boxcar from Lethbridge to Toronto as it docs to ship the processed rapcsced meal back from Toronto to Lethbridge,
The Address-Mr. Malone
Alberta. You have the same tonnage, the same car style and the same mileage, but a freight rate structure that is obviously biased against a certain region of Canada.
The Prime Minister shrugs his shoulders and wonders why the Canadian people are wrong in not being able to understand that the country will become divided. Obviously it is going to be divided so long as government policies are divided. This is not a country that is bent on being divided, but we do have a government that is bent on dividing people.
I have been looking at what is happening in terms of transportation. We are going to establish a new port policy. A new port at Churchill which will increase the grain flow out of that port during the production year would be something that would reduce the transportation costs of prairie farmers. It would increase to a tremendous degree the amount of income which could be generated within the prairies. There would be a decrease in transportation cost resulting from opening the port of Churchill to handle a much greater proportion of the grain produced in the prairie provinces. But the fact of the matter is that the government has reneged on its promise over and over again.
